3--- # Typeclasses
4-
5--- Chapter Poly introduced **parametric polymorphism**,
6--- declaring a type variable with no constraint on it:
7-
8-variable (α : Type)
9-
10--- Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1):
11---     Students will run across universes, though. When looking
12---     at List lemmas, for example, they will see things like:
13---
14---     `List.reverse.{u} {α : Type u} (as : List α) : List α`
15---
16---     Are we explaining these things somewhere, maybe in Poly
17---     ?
18-
19--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
20---     Yes, in Poly!
21-
22--- This lets us work with a type like `List α`, writing
23--- functions like `List.reverse` and `List.length` and proofs
24--- like `List.length_reverse`, which use only the list's
25--- structure and never inspect any particular `a : α`.
26-
27--- Sometimes, though, we want less freedom: rather than leaving
28--- `α` completely generic, we want to partially specify its
29--- behavior. In Lean, this is done through a form of "ad hoc
30--- polymorphism" called **typeclasses**. The concept originated
31--- in Haskell and is analogous to features you may know from
32--- other languages, such as traits in Rust.
33-
34--- ## Why We Need Typeclasses
35-
36--- Consider the following function, which checks whether a
37--- natural number occurs in a list:
38-
39-def List.elem_nat (a : Nat) (xs : List Nat) : Bool :=
40-  match xs with
41-  | [] => false
42-  | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_nat a tl
43-
44-theorem List.elem_nat_nil (a : Nat) : [].elem_nat a = false := rfl
45-
46-theorem List.elem_nat_cons (a b : Nat) (xs : List Nat) :
47-    (b :: xs).elem_nat a = bif a == b then true else elem_nat a xs := rfl
48-
49-#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 0
50-#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 1
51-#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 2
52-
53--- What if we want this to work for lists of *any* element
54--- type, not just `Nat`? Parametric polymorphism suggests
55--- simply replacing `Nat` with a type variable `α`, but that
56--- produces a puzzling error:
57-
58-sf_expect_failure
59-  def List.elem_poly {α : Type} (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
60-    match xs with
61-    | [] => false
62-    | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl
63-
64--- Lean is trying to use typeclasses to work out how `==`
65--- should behave on a value of type `α`. We'll see exactly why
66--- shortly; for now, here's one way to sidestep the problem:
67--- have the caller supply the equality test to use.
68-
69-def List.elem_poly_eq {α : Type} (eq : α → α → Bool) (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
70-  match xs with
71-  | [] => false
72-  | b :: tl => bif eq a b then true else elem_poly_eq eq a tl
73-
74-#eval [0, 1].elem_poly_eq Nat.beq 0
75-
76--- This works, but it's tedious: every caller has to know, and
77--- remember to supply, the right equality function.
78-
79--- Typeclasses automate this — instead of the programmer
80--- passing the function explicitly, Lean searches for one and
81--- provides it on its own. We specify something we want Lean to
82--- search for by declaring a `class` with the needed function
83--- as a field; a `class` is like an interface in Java or a
84--- trait in Rust. Particular implementations of that class,
85--- different ones for different types, are called *instances*.
86--- For functions that would use such instances, we specify the
87--- name of the class in a *instance implicit* on the
88--- polymorphic variable that the instance's function applies
89--- to. This directs Lean to rely on the class inside the
90--- function, and to find and fill in the appropriate instance
91--- when the function is called.
92-
93--- Here is what this looks like for `List.elem_poly`:
94-
95-def List.elem_poly {α : Type} [BEq α] (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
96-  match xs with
97-  | [] => false
98-  | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl
99-
100-theorem List.elem_poly_nil [BEq α] (a : α) : [].elem_poly a = false := rfl
101-
102-theorem List.elem_poly_cons [BEq α] (a b : α) (xs : List α) :
103-    (b :: xs).elem_poly a = bif a == b then true else elem_poly a xs := rfl
104-
105-#eval [0, 1].elem_poly 0
106-
107--- Comparing `List.elem_poly_eq` with `List.elem_poly`, we see
108--- three differences. First, `List.elem_poly_eq` takes an
109--- *explicit* parameter `eq`, whereas `List.elem_poly`
110--- specifies an instance implicit `[BEq α]`. The instance
111--- implicit indicates that an instance of `BEq` must be
112--- provided at call sites for the particular type `α` that is
113--- used. Second, whereas `List.elem_poly_eq` invokes parameter
114--- `eq` to test equality, `List.elem_poly` uses `==` instead.
115--- As Lists noted when we first used it, `==` on `Nat` comes
116--- from the `BEq` typeclass. Finally, whereas
117--- `[0, 1].elem_poly_eq Nat.beq 0` passes the equality function
118--- `Nat.beq` explicitly, in `[0, 1].elem_poly 0` Lean fills it
119--- in automatically based on the type `Nat` of the `List`.
120-
121--- Note to developers (xhalo32):
122---     This is technically incorrect, the instance `BEq Nat`,
123---     which comes from `DecidableEq`, does not contain
124---     `Nat.beq`. You can see in proofs of `List.elem_nat`
125---     versus `List.elem_poly_eq` versus `List.elem_poly` and
126---     how `Nat.beq` and `==` play different roles.
127-
128--- Going back to the earlier version of `List.elem_poly`,
129--- without the instance implicit, we can now understand the
130--- error message: `α` was fully generic — so the `==` in its
131--- body would have needed to work for *every* type `α`, and no
132--- single `BEq` instance can do that. So Lean's search failed.
133-
134--- Now it is time to dig into the details of what we have seen
135--- so far. We'll see exactly how `[BEq α]` gets filled in
136--- below, starting with how to define a typeclass in the first
137--- place.
138-
139--- ## Defining Your Own Typeclasses
140-
141--- `BEq` comes from Lean's standard library. Let's define a
142--- typeclass of our own, to see the mechanism — classes,
143--- instances, and synthesis — that made `==` resolve
144--- automatically above.
145-
146--- Suppose we want a function that returns the first element of
147--- a list, defaulting to a given value if the list is empty. As
148--- with `List.elem_poly_eq` above, here is a version that makes
149--- the default value an explicit parameter:
150-
151-def List.headOr_ex {α : Type} (defaultValue : α) (xs : List α) : α :=
152-  match xs with
153-  | [] => defaultValue
154-  | hd :: _ => hd
155-
156-#eval [1, 2, 3].headOr_ex 0
157-#eval ([] : List Nat).headOr_ex 0
158-
159--- This works, but again it's tedious: every caller has to
160--- supply an element of `α` to default to, even when there's an
161--- obvious choice based on the type of the things in the list,
162--- like `0` for `Nat`.
163-
164--- Getting Lean to fill in `defaultValue` automatically takes
165--- two things. One is marking the parameter as "searchable,"
166--- rather than something the caller always supplies explicitly.
167--- The other is giving Lean some information about what it
168--- should search *for*.
169-
170--- Considering the second problem first: The way to provide
171--- this information is to *name* the type-level concept we're
172--- after — the **default value** of a type. In particular, a
173--- `structure` (chapter Lists) is a good way to give a
174--- type-level concept a name; structures can also bundle
175--- together more than one piece of data, which will come in
176--- handy later, though we only need a single field here.
177-
178--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
179---     "type-level concept" doesn't say much to me here, and
180---     structures are *not* type-level things. (Well,
181---     `structure`s are, but *a* structure satisfying some
182---     `structure` declaration is not, if you see what I
183---     mean...)
184-
185--- Considering the first problem: we need to mark this
186--- particular structure as one Lean should search for
187--- automatically — not every `structure`-typed argument should
188--- be.
189-
190--- Let's build up to what wewant in two steps: first the
191--- naming, as a plain `structure`; then the marking, by
192--- upgrading it to a `class`. Here's the structure — we'll put
193--- it in its own namespace so we can reuse the name
194--- `DefaultValue` for the class version below:
195-
196-namespace DefaultValueScratch
197-
198-structure DefaultValue (α : Type) where
199-  value : α
200-
201--- A value of type `DefaultValue Nat` picks out a particular
202--- `Nat` to serve as the type's default: it's built the same
203--- way any structure is, by supplying a `Nat` for the `value`
204--- field:
205-
206-def natDefault : DefaultValue Nat where
207-  value := 1
208-
209-example : natDefault.value = 1 := rfl
210-
211-end DefaultValueScratch
212-
213--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
214---     Maybe the example is not needed?
215-
216--- Now for the marking: we need to tell Lean that
217--- `DefaultValue` is the sort of structure it should search for
218--- automatically, the way it needs to for `List.headOr_ex`'s
219--- `defaultValue` argument. We do this by writing `class` in
220--- place of `structure`:
221-
222-class DefaultValue (α : Type) where
223-  value : α
224-
225--- We then provide values of this type a bit differently.
226--- Instead of `def`, we use `instance`:
227-
228-instance instDefaultValueNat : DefaultValue Nat where
229-  value := 1
230-
231--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
232---     Boldface, or italic? We should write down a rule in
233---     STYLE.md!
234-
235--- Lean can now find this instance on its own, via **typeclass
236--- synthesis** (or **typeclass inference**) — the same process
237--- that found `BEq Nat` earlier. That means we can rewrite
238--- `List.headOr_ex` the same way we rewrote `List.elem_poly_eq`
239--- into `List.elem_poly` above, replacing the explicit
240--- `defaultValue` parameter with an instance implicit:
241-
242-def List.headOr {α : Type} [DefaultValue α] (xs : List α) : α :=
243-  match xs with
244-  | [] => DefaultValue.value
245-  | hd :: _ => hd
246-
247-#eval [1, 2, 3].headOr
248-#eval ([] : List Nat).headOr
249-
250-example : DefaultValue.value = (1 : Nat) := rfl
251-
252--- Notice that we refer to `DefaultValue.value` alone, with no
253--- instance named. Because the expression equates
254--- `DefaultValue.value` with the `Nat` `1`, Lean selects
255--- `instDefaultValueNat`, the instance for `DefaultValue Nat`.
256--- We know this because we are able to prove that
257--- `DefaultValue.value` is equal to 1.
258-
259--- Let's declare a second instance, for `Int`, the type of
260--- integers `... -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ...`:
261-
262-instance instDefaultValueInt : DefaultValue Int where
263-  value := -1
264-
265--- Now, Lean can infer instances for both types, including
266--- inside `List.headOr`:
267-
268-example : DefaultValue.value = (1 : Nat) := rfl
269-example : DefaultValue.value = (-1 : Int) := rfl
270-example : ([] : List Nat).headOr = 1 := rfl
271-example : ([] : List Int).headOr = -1 := rfl
272-
273--- Synthesis infers instances we could have specified
274--- explicitly:
275-
276-example : instDefaultValueNat.value = (1 : Nat) := rfl
277-example : instDefaultValueInt.value = (-1 : Int) := rfl
278-
279--- The option `pp.all` shows which instance Lean picked:
280-
281-set_option pp.all true in
282-#check (DefaultValue.value : Nat)
283-
284--- @DefaultValue.value Nat instDefaultValueNat : Nat
285-
286-set_option pp.all true in
287-#check (DefaultValue.value : Int)
288-
289--- @DefaultValue.value Int instDefaultValueInt : Int
290-
291--- This reveals `instDefaultValueNat` and `instDefaultValueInt`
292--- as the instances Lean picked. The `#synth` command runs the
293--- same search directly:
294-
295-#synth DefaultValue Nat
296-
297--- instDefaultValueNat
298-
299--- For a typeclass like `DefaultValue` that carries data — a
300--- term, such as the `1` above, rather than only proofs (which
301--- we will see below) — we expect at most one instance per
302--- type, so this search has a unique answer.
303-
304--- We'll put `DefaultValue`'s standard-library cousin,
305--- `Inhabited`, to work later in this chapter, when we define
306--- maps that need a default value for a generic type. First,
307--- though, let's go back to `List.elem_poly` and see how its
308--- `[BEq α]` argument actually gets resolved.
309-
310--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
311---     Is it a cousin, or a duplicate?
312-
313--- ## Using Typeclasses
314-
315--- Let's check what `==` meant for `List.elem_nat`, with
316--- notation display turned off:
317-
318-set_option pp.notation false in
319-#check 1 == 2
320-
321--- Rather than `Nat.beq`, `==` turns out to be notation for
322--- `BEq.beq`, a field of exactly the kind of typeclass we just
323--- learned to define:
324-
325--- class BEq (α : Type u) where
326---   /-- Boolean equality, notated as `a == b`. -/
327---   beq : α → α → Bool
328-
329--- Writing `a == b` makes Lean search for an **instance** of
330--- `BEq` for the type of `a` and `b`, the same way it searched
331--- for a `DefaultValue` instance above. For `Nat`, that
332--- instance is:
333-
334-instance (priority := low) : BEq Nat where
335-  beq := Nat.beq
336-
337--- This is the instance Lean supplies for `[BEq α]` when
338--- `List.elem_poly` is called on a `List Nat` — no different
339--- from Lean choosing `instDefaultValueNat` for
340--- `DefaultValue.value` earlier when it was equated with
341--- `(1 : Nat)`.
342-
343--- ### Exercise (1 star): List.elem_poly_eq_elem_nat ⭐
344-
345--- Prove that `List.elem_poly` agrees with `List.elem_nat` when
346--- specialized to natural numbers.
347-
348-theorem List.elem_poly_eq_elem_nat (xs : List Nat) (n : Nat) : xs.elem_poly n = xs.elem_nat n := by
349-  sorry

351--- ## Proof-Carrying Typeclasses
352-
353--- The above examples enforce no conditions on the data an
354--- instance may carry — any value of the right type will do.
355--- But sometimes enforcing constraints on data is useful. For
356--- example, suppose we want to specify that a type has not just
357--- a single element, but two. Here is a first attempt:
358-
359-sf_experiment
360-  class HasTwoIncomplete (α : Type) where
361-    one : α
362-    two : α
363-
364--- Unfortunately, this specification isn't precise because it
365--- allows `one` and `two` to refer to the same term.
366--- Fortunately, Lean's typeclasses can carry proofs along with
367--- data, so we can write the following to enforce that `one`
368--- and `two` are distinct.
369-
370-class HasTwo (α : Type) where
371-  one : α
372-  two : α
373-  one_neq_two : one ≠ two
374-
375--- Declaring instances works in much the same way as before,
376--- except that now the `HasTwo.one_neq_two` field requires a
377--- proof:
378-
379-instance : HasTwo Nat where
380-  one := 1
381-  two := 2
382-  one_neq_two := by intro contra; contradiction
383-
384--- In most languages that support typeclasses (or traits) it is
385--- not possible to formally enforce laws such as `one_neq_two`.
386--- Thus it falls to the author to check, informally, that any
387--- required invariants are satisfied, which can lead to bugs.
388-
389--- ### Exercise (1 star): HasThree ⭐
390-
391--- Following the pattern of `DefaultValue` and `HasTwo`, define
392--- a class `HasThree` that specifies a type with at least three
393--- distinct elements, and give an instance of it for `Nat`.
394-
395-class HasThree (α : Type) where
396-  one : α
397-  two : α
398-  three : α
399-  one_neq_two : one ≠ two
400-  -- FILL IN HERE
401-
402-instance : HasThree Nat where
403-  one := 1
404-  two := 2
405-  three := 3
406-  one_neq_two := sorry
407-  -- FILL IN HERE

409--- ## Maps
410-
411--- *Maps* (or "dictionaries") are ubiquitous data structures
412--- both in ordinary programming and in the theory of
413--- programming languages; we're going to need them in many
414--- places in later volumes.
415-
416--- We'll define two flavors of maps: *total maps*, which
417--- include a "default" element to be returned when a key being
418--- looked up doesn't exist, and *partial maps*, which instead
419--- return an option to indicate success or failure. Partial
420--- maps are defined in terms of total maps, using `none` as the
421--- default element.
422-
423--- ### Key and Value Types
424-
425--- To define maps, we first need a type for the keys that we
426--- will use to index into our maps and a type for the values
427--- the maps return. Instead of choosing concrete types for
428--- these, we will use type variables.
429-
430--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
431---     Should we perhaps refer back to where the `variable`
432---     declaration is explained? (I guess in Poly, but which
433---     section?)
434---
435---     More generally, the exposition gets a little thick from
436---     here to the next section header.
437-
438-variable {α : Type} {β : Type} [BEq α] [ReflBEq α] [LawfulBEq α]
439-
440-set_option linter.unusedSectionVars false
441-
442--- Here, `α` is the type of the keys and `β` the corresponding
443--- values. In addition to `BEq`, which we have already seen,
444--- the key type `α` requires instances of the `ReflBEq` and
445--- `LawfulBEq` typeclasses:
446-
447--- /-- `ReflBEq α` says that the `BEq` implementation is reflexive. -/
448--- class ReflBEq (α) [BEq α] : Prop where
449---   /-- `==` is reflexive, that is, `(a == a) = true`. -/
450---   protected rfl {a : α} : a == a
451-
452--- /--
453--- A Boolean equality test coincides with propositional equality.
454-
455--- In other words:
456---  * `a == b` implies `a = b`.
457---  * `a == a` is true.
458--- -/
459--- class LawfulBEq (α : Type u) [BEq α] : Prop extends ReflBEq α where
460---   /-- If `a == b` evaluates to `true`, then `a` and `b` are equal in the logic. -/
461---   eq_of_beq : {a b : α} → a == b → a = b
462-
463--- These classes refine `BEq`, specifying that (`==`) is
464--- reflexive and coincides with proposition equality `=`.
465-
466--- We place no constraints on the value type `β`.
467-
468--- ### Total Maps
469-
470--- The Lists chapter introduced a partial map abstraction,
471--- `PartialMap`, with a `find` function for lookup, based on
472--- lists of key-value pairs. Here, we are going to build a map
473--- abstraction using functions instead. The advantage of this
474--- representation is that it offers a more *extensional* view
475--- of maps, as we saw with functions in the Logic chapter: two
476--- maps that respond to every query in the same way will be
477--- represented as exactly the same function, rather than just
478--- as "equivalent" list structures. This simplifies proofs that
479--- use maps.
480-
481--- Note to developers (Claude):
482---     This paragraph previously wrote `{tech}_extensional_`,
483---     but that failed to build here with
484---     `No term def with key "extensional"`. The `{tech}` role
485---     emits a **reference** to a technical term that must
486---     resolve to a matching `{deftech}` definition; the only
487---     `{deftech}_extensional_` lives in the Logic chapter, and
488---     Verso's tech-term index isn't shared with this chapter's
489---     build, so the key can't be found. We flattened it to
490---     plain emphasis (`_extensional_`), matching how Logic
491---     itself renders in the generated `.lean`. Alternative
492---     fixes if we want a live link: add a local `{deftech}`
493---     for the term in this chapter, or arrange for
494---     cross-chapter `{tech}` references to resolve in a
495---     whole-book build.
496-
497-def TotalMap (α : Type) (β : Type) := α → β
498-
499-namespace TotalMap
500-
501--- Intuitively, a total map over an element type `β` is just a
502--- function that can be looked up using a corresponding
503--- `a : α`.
504-
505--- In order to declare a default value of `β` we will use the
506--- `Inhabited` typeclass, which is the standard library's
507--- implementation of our `DefaultValue` example from above:
508-
509-variable [Inhabited β]
510-
511--- The function `TotalMap.empty` yields an empty total map,
512--- given a default element; this map always returns the default
513--- element when applied to any key.
514-
515-def empty : TotalMap α β := fun _ ↦ default
516-
517--- Just as declaring `BEq`/`DefaultValue` instances above
518--- hooked `==` and `DefaultValue.value` up to our types, we can
519--- declare an instance of the standard library's
520--- `EmptyCollection` typeclass to associate `∅` with this empty
521--- map.
522-
523-instance : EmptyCollection (TotalMap α β) where
524-  emptyCollection := TotalMap.empty
525-
526--- Here, for example, is an empty map that takes `Nat` keys to
527--- `Nat` values:
528-
529-def emptyNatMap : TotalMap Nat Nat := ∅
530-
531--- Since a map is a function, we can apply it to a key to get
532--- out the corresponding value, like so:
533-
534-example : emptyNatMap 1 = default := rfl
535-example : emptyNatMap 2 = 0 := rfl
536-
537--- (For `Nat` the `default` is `0`.)
538-
539--- #### Getting Elements
540-
541--- While `TotalMap`s happen to be implemented as functions
542--- under the hood, we would prefer not to expose this fact in
543--- their public interface. Accordingly, we define new
544--- operations for querying and updating mappings. As a first
545--- attempt at a query operation, playing the role that `find`
546--- played for the Lists chapter's list-based maps, we could
547--- define a function `getElem` for getting the value associated
548--- with a key:
549-
550-sf_experiment
551-  def getElem (m : TotalMap α β) (a: α) := m a
552-  
553-  example : getElem emptyNatMap 2 = 0 := rfl
554-
555--- To make element-getting lighter weight, let's define
556--- notation so we can write `emptyNatMap[2]` rather than
557--- `getElem emptyNatMap`. We could notate `getElem` directly —
558--- we'll do exactly that for `update` below — but here we'll
559--- instead make "getting an element" its own typeclass,
560--- `MyGetElem`, and notate *instances* of it. Doing so means
561--- `m[a]` resolves to `MyGetElem.getElem m a` for any type with
562--- a `MyGetElem` instance, not just `TotalMap`.
563-
564--- Using typeclasses to define notation is typical in Lean when
565--- the same notation is useful for many different types. We
566--- have seen the approach already with `==`: writing `a == b`
567--- is notation for `BEq.beq`, resolved by instance search for
568--- whatever type `a` and `b` have. We also just saw overloaded
569--- notation for `EmptyCollection` above, where `∅` is notation
570--- for `EmptyCollection.emptyCollection`. Our typeclass
571--- `MyGetElem` is a simpler version of the standard library's
572--- `GetElem` typeclass, which has many instances such as
573--- `Array`, `List`, and `Vector`. We develop it to illustrate
574--- the notation-as-typeclass approach.
575-
576-end TotalMap
577-
578--- The `MyGetElem` typeclass takes three type parameters: the
579--- map implementation, its keys, and its values.
580-
581-class MyGetElem (coll : Type) (idx : Type) (elem : outParam Type) where
582-  getElem (xs : coll) (i : idx) : elem
583-
584--- (Don't worry about the `outParam` qualifier; it is a hint to
585--- Lean that helps typeclass inference.)
586-
587--- The appropriate instance of `MyGetElem` for our `TotalMap`
588--- is:
589-
590-variable [Inhabited β]
591-instance : MyGetElem (TotalMap α β) α β where
592-  getElem m a := m a
593-
594--- Now we can associate the bracket syntax with
595--- `MyGetElem.getElem`. We've defined custom notation before —
596--- `::` and `[...]` for lists (chapter Lists, including an
597--- `app_unexpander` for printing `[...]`-notation lists back
598--- out), or `+`/`*`/`==` for arithmetic — but always with
599--- `infixl`/`infixr` or `scoped macro`; this is the first time
600--- we reach for the more general `notation`/`macro_rules` forms
601--- for getting the `m[a]` syntax to work. (Don't worry about
602--- following the mechanism in detail — the `macro_rules` and
603--- the `app_unexpander` below are minor technicalities.)
604-
605--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
606---     Can we point people to where they can read about these
607---     things if they are interested?
608-
609-namespace MyGetElem
610-
611-scoped macro_rules | `($xs[$i]) => `(getElem $xs $i)
612-
613-@[app_unexpander getElem]
614-def unexpandGetElem : Lean.PrettyPrinter.Unexpander

643---     As per the discussion in

651---     The reverse direction of `getElem_def` is provided as a

654---     `example (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) : m a = m[a] := by

656---       -- dsimp -- doesn't work (nothing happens)
657---       -- rw [apply_eq_getElem] -- doesn't work: The pattern to be substituted is a metavariable (`?m ?a`) in this equality: ?m ?a = ?m[?a]

665---     `[Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite] apply_eq_getElem:1000:
666---           m a
667---         ==>
668---           m[a]

670---           m[a]
671---         ==>
672---           (MyGetElem.getElem m)[a]
673---     [Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite] apply_eq_getElem:1000:
674---           (MyGetElem.getElem m)[a]
675---         ==>
676---           (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m))[a]

678---           (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m))[a]
679---         ==>
680---           (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m)))[a]
681---     [Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite] apply_eq_getElem:1000:
682---           (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m)))[a]
683---         ==>...`

685---     So I think the issue here is that the LHS m a is too
686---     board, causing this lemma repeating itself. First we
687---     have `m a => m[a], but m[a]` is defeq to
688---     (MyGetElem.getElem m) a, and nevertheless we require m
689---     to be a TotalMap, a TotalMap is defeq to α → β. So this
690---     lemma applies again --
691---     `(MyGetElem.getElem m) a => (MyGetElem.getElem m)[a]`

695--- #### Updating Elements
696-
697--- Now we turn to the `update` function, which takes a map `m`,
698--- a key `a`, and a value `b` and returns a new map that takes
699--- `a` to `b` and takes every other key to whatever `m` does.
700--- We do this by wrapping a new map function around the old
701--- one.
702-
703-def update (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) : TotalMap α β :=
704-  fun a' => bif a == a' then b else m[a']
705-
706--- This definition is a nice example of higher-order
707--- programming: `update` takes a function `m` and yields a new
708--- function `fun a' => ...` that behaves like the desired map.
709-
710--- For example, we can build a map taking `String` to `Bool`,
711--- where `"foo"` and `"bar"` are mapped to `true` and every
712--- other key is mapped to `false`, like this:
713-
714-def exampleMap :=
715-  (∅ : TotalMap String Bool)
716-    |>.update "foo" true
717-    |>.update "bar" true
718-
719--- Here `|>` is Lean's **pipe** notation: `x |>.f y` means
720--- `x.f y`, letting us chain a sequence of function or method
721--- calls left to right without nested parentheses.
722-
723--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
724---     Should we introduce this notation earlier? (Are there
725---     good places to use it earlier?)
726-
727--- We also introduce a notation for updating maps — this time,
728--- rather than going through a typeclass and its own
729--- `notation`/`macro_rules` machinery as we did for
730--- `MyGetElem`, we write a `notation` that references
731--- `TotalMap.update` directly. Unlike indexing, `update`
732--- doesn't need to work generically across container types
733--- (there's no standard-library operation like `GetElem` that
734--- we're mirroring here), so the simpler, direct route
735--- suffices.
736-
737-notation a:55 " →ₜ " b:55 " ; " m:55 => TotalMap.update m a b
738-
739-theorem update_def (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) :
740-  a →ₜ b ; m = fun a' => bif a == a' then b else m[a'] := rfl
741-
742--- We can hide the last case when it is empty:
743-
744-notation a:55 " →ₜ " b:55 => TotalMap.update ∅ a b
745-
746--- The `examplemap` above can now be defined as follows:
747-
748-def exampleMap' : TotalMap String Bool := "bar" →ₜ true ; "foo" →ₜ true ; ∅
749-def exampleMap'' : TotalMap String Bool := "bar" →ₜ true ; "foo" →ₜ true
750-
751--- This completes the definition of total maps.
752-
753-example : exampleMap = exampleMap' := rfl
754-example : exampleMap' = exampleMap'' := rfl
755-
756-example : exampleMap'["baz"] = false := rfl
757-example : exampleMap'["foo"] = true := rfl
758-example : exampleMap'["quux"] = false := rfl
759-example : exampleMap'["bar"] = true := rfl

761--- When we use maps in later volumes, we'll need several
762--- fundamental facts about how they behave.

764--- Even if you don't work the following exercises, make sure
765--- you thoroughly understand the statements of the lemmas!
766-
767--- (Some of the proofs require the functional extensionality
768--- axiom `funext`, discussed in the Logic chapter.)
769-
770--- First, the empty map returns its default element for all
771--- keys:
772-
773-theorem getElem_empty (a : α) : (∅ : TotalMap α β)[a] = default := rfl
774-
775--- Next, if we update a map `m` at a key `a` with a new value
776--- `b` and then look up `a` in the map resulting from the
777--- `update`, we get back `b`:
778-
779-theorem update_eq (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) : (a →ₜ b ; m)[a] = b := by
780-  rw [update_def, getElem_def, ReflBEq.rfl, cond_true]
781-
782--- On the other hand, if we update a map `m` at a key `a₁` and
783--- then look up a *different* key `a₂` in the resulting map, we
784--- get the same result that `m` would have given:
785-
786--- ### Exercise (2 stars): update_neq ⭐⭐
787-
788-theorem update_neq {m : TotalMap α β} {a₁ a₂ : α} (h : a₁ ≠ a₂) (b : β) :
789-    (a₁ →ₜ b ; m)[a₂] = m[a₂] := by
790-  sorry
791-
792--- The two remaining facts are equalities *between maps*, so we
793--- first need to say when two maps are equal. Since a total map
794--- is implemented as a function, this is exactly the functional
795--- extensionality principle (`funext`) from the Logic chapter:
796--- two maps are equal when they agree at every key. Recording
797--- it once, for maps, and tagging it `@[ext]` lets the `ext`
798--- tactic reduce a goal `m₁ = m₂` to the pointwise one in the
799--- proofs below.
800-
801-@[ext]
802-theorem ext {m₁ m₂ : TotalMap α β} (h : ∀ a : α, m₁[a] = m₂[a]) : m₁ = m₂ := funext h
803-
804--- If we update a map `m` at a key `a` with a value `b₁` and
805--- then update again with the same key `a` and another value
806--- `b₂`, the resulting map behaves the same (gives the same
807--- result when applied to any key) as the simpler map obtained

874--- ### Notation for Concrete Maps
875-
876--- Wouldn't it be nice if we could use a more natural notation
877--- for concrete maps like `{ "bar" ↦ true, "foo" ↦ true }`? To
878--- accomplish this we define a simple structure that consists
879--- of a key and a value along with `↦` notation for it.
880-
881-/--
882-A key-value pair with `↦` syntax.
883--/
884-@[ext]
885-structure KVPair (K : Type) (V : Type) where
886-  key : K
887-  value : V
888-
889-namespace KVPair
890-scoped notation k " ↦ " v => KVPair.mk k v
891-end KVPair
892-
893-open scoped KVPair
894-
895--- Next, we declare `Insert` and `Singleton` instances — the
896--- standard-library typeclasses behind the `{x, y, ...}` and
897--- `{x}` collection-literal notation that `List`, `Finset`, and
898--- other stdlib containers already support — so that `TotalMap`
899--- can use it too.
900-
901-namespace TotalMap
902-
903-variable [Inhabited β]
904-
905-instance : Insert (KVPair α β) (TotalMap α β) where
906-  insert kv m := kv.key →ₜ kv.value ; m
907-
908-instance : Singleton (KVPair α β) (TotalMap α β) where
909-  singleton kv := insert kv ∅
910-
911-instance : LawfulSingleton (KVPair α β) (TotalMap α β) where
912-  insert_empty_eq _ := rfl
913-
914-end TotalMap
915-

917-
918-example : ({ "bar" ↦ true, "foo" ↦ true }) = "bar" →ₜ true ; "foo" →ₜ true ; ∅ := rfl
919-
920-example : ({ "foo" ↦ true } : TotalMap String Bool)["foo"] = true := rfl
921-
922-example : ({ 1 ↦ 2, 1 ↦ 3 } : TotalMap Nat Nat)[1] = 2 := rfl

924--- The reason we need to explicitly specify the type of the map
925--- is that Lean doesn't know what type of collection
926--- `{ "foo" ↦ true }` is without type hints, as we can see with
927--- `#check`:
928-
929-#check { "foo" ↦ true }
930-
931--- {"foo" ↦ true} : ?m.4
932-
933--- The type shows a `?m.4`, which indicates that Lean can't
934--- infer the type. A type which can't be inferred doesn't have
935--- any type classes like `MyGetElem`, so typeclass resolution
936--- gets stuck in the following example:
937-
938-sf_expect_failure
939-  example : ({ "foo" ↦ true })["foo"] = true := rfl

941--- ### Partial Maps
942-
943--- Note to developers (Niklas Halonen @xhalo32):
944---     We should spend some time discussing differences between
945---     the inductive approach in Lists.lean and the approach
946---     here. The inductive approach could be made polymorphic
947---     and proven to be equivalent with partial maps (I
948---     believe), so the point is not that the maps are
949---     extensionally different. A question (that I don't have
950---     an answer to) is then: what makes the new partial map
951---     better?
952-
953--- Lastly, we define *partial maps* on top of total maps. A
954--- partial map with elements of type `β` is simply a total map
955--- with elements of type `Option β`, whose default element is
956--- `none`.
957-
958-structure PartialMap (α : Type) (β : Type) where
959-  /-- The underlying total map. Lean always generates a public projection for a structure
960-  field, so `inner` is technically accessible, but it isn't part of the intended interface:
961-  use `PartialMap.toTotal` instead, so there's exactly one sanctioned way to get at it. -/
962-  inner : TotalMap α (Option β)
963-
964-instance : EmptyCollection (PartialMap α β) where
965-  emptyCollection := { inner := ∅ }
966-
967-def PartialMap.toTotal (m : PartialMap α β) : TotalMap α (Option β) := m.inner
968-
969-instance : MyGetElem (PartialMap α β) α (Option β) where
970-  getElem m a := m.toTotal[a]
971-
972-theorem getElem_def (m : PartialMap α β) (a : α) : m[a] = m.toTotal[a] := rfl
973-
974--- Remember that we discussed earlier with total maps that
975--- using function application exposes the implementation, and
976--- that's why we introduced a new notation `MyGetElem`? Here we
977--- take that concept to a new level, and instead of using a
978--- `def` for partial maps, like this...
979-
980---   def PartialMap (α : Type) (β : Type) := TotalMap α (Option β)`
981-
982--- ...we define partial maps as a structure containing just a
983--- total map. This more strongly hides the fact that it's a
984--- total map.
985-
986--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
987---     If this way is better, then why didn't we do it for
988---     total maps too? Just for the sake of explaining two
989---     different mechanisms? We should explain our reasoning.
990---
991---     Claude: One possible reason — `TotalMap` is deliberately
992---     left as a bare function type because that transparency
993---     is the point of the Total Maps section: it's what lets
994---     two maps that answer every query the same way count as
995---     **literally** the same value, giving the extensional
996---     view of map equality. `PartialMap` doesn't need to make
997---     that same point, so it's free to hide the representation
998---     more thoroughly here. This is a guess at the original
999---     reasoning, not a confirmed answer — flagging it here for
1000---     discussion rather than asserting it in the chapter text.
1001-
1002--- Now, the type system doesn't consider `PartialMap α β` to be
1003--- definitionally equal to `TotalMap α (Option β)`, so the
1004--- following equality doesn't type check:
1005-
1006-sf_expect_failure
1007-  example : (∅ : PartialMap α β) = (∅ : TotalMap α (Option β)) := by rfl
1008-

1010---   ∅
1011--- has type
1012---   TotalMap α (Option β)
1013--- but is expected to have type
1014---   PartialMap α β

1017---     The Maps chapter removed the `optionCoe` instance for
1018---     the duration of its partial-map development
1019---     (`attribute [-instance] optionCoe`, restored at
1020---     `end PartialMap`), on the grounds that a coercion from

1024---     metadata coercion (`Tag → Option Tag`) fails at

1027---
1028---     We have not carried that over — nothing here needs it
1029---     and it is not clear it is wanted. Decide whether to
1030---     reinstate it.

1032--- Updating a partial map at a key means storing a `some` value
1033--- there. To update, we create a new partial map from
1034--- `a →ₜ some b ; m.toTotal` by wrapping it in angle brackets,
1035--- i.e. using the anonymous constructor syntax. This is
1036--- equivalent to writing
1037--- `{ inner := a →ₜ some b ; m.toTotal }`. We also introduce a
1038--- similar notation for it as for total maps.
1039-
1040-namespace PartialMap
1041-
1042-def update (m : PartialMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) : PartialMap α β :=
1043-  ⟨a →ₜ some b ; m.toTotal⟩
1044-
1045-notation a:55 " →ₚ " b:55 " ; " m:55 => PartialMap.update m a b
1046-
1047-notation a:55 " →ₚ " b:55 => PartialMap.update ∅ a b
1048-
1049-def examplePmap : PartialMap String Bool := "Church" →ₚ true ; "Turing" →ₚ false

1051--- Next, we provide some fundamental properties about
1052--- `toTotal`:
1053-
1054-theorem toTotal_empty : (∅ : PartialMap α β).toTotal = (∅ : TotalMap α (Option β)) := rfl
1055-
1056-theorem toTotal_update (m : PartialMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) :
1057-    (a →ₚ b ; m).toTotal = a →ₜ some b ; m.toTotal := rfl
1058-
1059--- As an example, here's how we can use these on some concrete
1060--- maps:
1061-
1062-example : (2 →ₚ 3)[2] = some 3 := by
1063-  rw [getElem_def, toTotal_update, toTotal_empty, TotalMap.getElem_def]
1064-  rfl
1065-
1066--- This also holds by definition (`rfl`), since all the
1067--- rewrites in the above proof do the computation step-by-step.
1068-
1069-example : (2 →ₚ 3)[2] = some 3 := by rfl

1071--- Next, we lift all of the basic lemmas about total maps to
1072--- partial maps. To do this we should first prove an
1073--- extensionality lemma about partial maps. To prove
1074--- extensionality, we employ injectivity of `PartialMap`'s
1075--- constructor `mk` using `mk.injEq`.
1076-
1077-theorem toTotal_eq_iff (m₁ m₂ : PartialMap α β) : m₁.toTotal = m₂.toTotal ↔ m₁ = m₂ := by
1078-  rw [mk.injEq]
1079-  rfl
1080-
1081-@[ext]
1082-theorem ext {m₁ m₂ : PartialMap α β} (h : ∀ a : α, m₁[a] = m₂[a]) : m₁ = m₂ := by
1083-  rw [← toTotal_eq_iff]
1084-  exact TotalMap.ext h
1085-
1086--- Now, let's lift the `TotalMap` lemmas:
1087-
1088-theorem getElem_empty (a : α) : (∅ : PartialMap α β)[a] = none := by
1089-  rw [getElem_def, toTotal_empty, TotalMap.getElem_empty, Option.default_eq_none]
1090-
1091-theorem update_eq (m : PartialMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) : (a →ₚ b ; m)[a] = some b := by
1092-  rw [getElem_def, toTotal_update, TotalMap.update_eq]
1093-
1094-theorem update_neq {m : PartialMap α β} {a₁ a₂ : α} (h : a₁ ≠ a₂) (b : β) :
1095-    (a₁ →ₚ b ; m)[a₂] = m[a₂] := by
1096-  dsimp [getElem_def, toTotal_update]
1097-  rw [TotalMap.update_neq h]
1098-
1099-theorem update_shadow (m : PartialMap α β) (a : α) (b₁ b₂ : β) :
1100-    (a →ₚ b₂ ; a →ₚ b₁ ; m) = (a →ₚ b₂ ; m) := by
1101-  apply ext
1102-  intro x
1103-  dsimp [getElem_def, toTotal_update]
1104-  rw [TotalMap.update_shadow]
1105-
1106-theorem update_same {m : PartialMap α β} {a : α} {b : β} (h : m[a] = some b) :
1107-    (a →ₚ b ; m) = m := by
1108-  apply ext
1109-  intro x
1110-  dsimp [getElem_def, toTotal_update]
1111-  rw [← h, getElem_def, TotalMap.update_same]
1112-
1113-theorem update_permute {m : PartialMap α β} {a₁ a₂ : α} {b₁ b₂ : β} (h : a₁ ≠ a₂) :
1114-    (a₁ →ₚ b₁ ; a₂ →ₚ b₂ ; m) = (a₂ →ₚ b₂ ; a₁ →ₚ b₁ ; m) := by
1115-  apply ext
1116-  intro x
1117-  dsimp [getElem_def, toTotal_update]
1118-  rw [TotalMap.update_permute h]

1122-instance : Insert (KVPair α β) (PartialMap α β) where
1123-  insert kv m := kv.key →ₚ kv.value ; m
1124-
1125-instance : Singleton (KVPair α β) (PartialMap α β) where
1126-  singleton kv := insert kv ∅
1127-
1128-instance : LawfulSingleton (KVPair α β) (PartialMap α β) where
1129-  insert_empty_eq _ := rfl

1232--- We've seen two different ways of expressing logical claims
1233--- in Lean: with booleans (of type `Bool`), and with
1234--- propositions (of type `Prop`).
1235-
1236--- Here are the key differences between `Bool` and `Prop`:
1237-
1238--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
1239---     Check formatting:
1240-
1241--- - ⠀
1242--- - `Bool`
1243--- - `Prop`
1244--- - decidable?
1245--- - yes
1246--- - no
1247--- - useable with `match`?
1248--- - yes
1249--- - no
1250--- - works with `rewrite` tactic?
1251--- - no
1252--- - yes
1253-
1254--- The crucial difference between the two worlds is
1255--- decidability. Every (closed) Lean expression of type `Bool`
1256--- can be simplified in a finite number of steps to either
1257--- `true` or `false` — i.e., there is a terminating mechanical
1258--- procedure for deciding whether or not it is true.
1259-
1260--- This means that, for example, the type `Nat → Bool` is
1261--- inhabited only by functions that, given a `Nat`, always
1262--- yield either `true` or `false` in finite time; and this, in
1263--- turn, means (by a standard computability argument) that
1264--- there is no function in `Nat → Bool` that checks whether a
1265--- given number is the code of a terminating Turing machine.
1266-
1267--- By contrast, the type `Prop` includes both decidable and
1268--- undecidable mathematical propositions; in particular, the
1269--- type `Nat → Prop` does contain functions representing
1270--- properties like "the nth Turing machine halts." The second
1271--- row in the table follows directly from this essential
1272--- difference. To evaluate a pattern match (or conditional) on
1273--- a boolean, we need to know whether the scrutinee evaluates
1274--- to `true` or `false`; this only works for `Bool`, not
1275--- `Prop`.
1276-
1277--- The third row highlights an important practical difference:
1278--- equality functions like `Nat.beq` that return a boolean
1279--- cannot be used directly to justify rewriting with the
1280--- rewrite tactic; propositional equality is required for this.
1281--- Since `Prop` includes both decidable and undecidable
1282--- properties, we have two options when we want to formalize a
1283--- property that happens to be decidable: we can express it
1284--- either as a boolean computation or as a function into Prop.
1285-
1286--- As an example, we can write
1287-
1288-unseal isEven in
1289-example : isEven 42 := rfl
1290-
1291--- or that there exists some `k` such that `42 = double k`.
1292-
1293-unseal double in
1294-example : Even 42 := by exists 21
1295-
1296--- Of course, it would be deeply strange if these two
1297--- characterizations of evenness did not describe the same set
1298--- of natural numbers!
1299-

1301--- helper lemmas.

1308-  | succ n ih =>

1310-    exact ih

1331--- computation `isEven n` is reflected in the truth of the

1348--- So what should we do in situations where some claim could be
1349--- formalized as either a proposition or a boolean computation?

1356--- otherwise. As an example, consider trying to write a

11--- Copied from `SubVerso.Compat` to avoid making generated projects depend on verso.
12--- We want to have info state and messages available right after the elaboration,
13--- so we need to disable `Elab.async` which would let diagnostics produced asynchronously
14--- through spanshot tasks.
15-private def commandWithoutAsync (act : CommandElabM Unit) : CommandElabM Unit := do
16-  match (← get).scopes with
17-  | [] => act
18-  | h :: t =>
19-    let mut orig : Option Bool := none
20-    try
21-      orig := h.opts.get? `Elab.async
22-      modify fun s => { s with scopes := { h with opts := h.opts.setBool `Elab.async false } :: t }
23-      act
24-    finally
25-      if let h :: t := (← get).scopes then
26-        let opts := orig.map (h.opts.setBool `Elab.async) |>.getD (h.opts.erase `Elab.async)
27-        modify fun s => { s with scopes := { h with opts := opts } :: t }
28-
29-private def withRestoringState (keepMsgs : Bool) (m : CommandElabM Unit) : CommandElabM Unit := do
30-  let savedState ← get
31-  try
32-    m
33-  finally
34-    let state ← get
35-    set { savedState with
36-      -- Preserve the info tree
37-      infoState := state.infoState
38-      messages := if keepMsgs then state.messages else savedState.messages }

40-namespace IndentedCommands

42-/-! # Block Commands Parser
43-  Parse an indented command block. Commands are separated by new lines.
44-  Since we want to capture parsing errors in `sf_expect_failure`,
45-  we can't use Lean command parser directly in our command's syntax,
46-  because any parsing error occurred would fail `sf_expect_failure` itself.
47-  One possible solution is to first parse the whole indented body as raw syntax,
48-  and then run Lean's command parser followed by command elaboration.
49--/
50-
51-open Parser
52-
53-private def rawLineEndFn : ParserFn :=
54-  eoiFn <|> satisfyFn (· == '\n') "line break"
55-
56-/-- Consumes everything until the next newline and then consumes the newline itself. -/
57-private def rawLineFn : ParserFn :=
58-  takeUntilFn (· == '\n') >> rawLineEndFn
59-
60-/- For each line after the first body line, consumes leading whitespaces.
61-  If it's blank, consumes the newline; otherwise consumes the line
62-  requiring the indentation.
63--/
64-private def rawIndentedLineFn : ParserFn := atomicFn <|
65-  takeWhileFn (· == ' ') >>
66-  (satisfyFn (· == '\n') "line break" <|>
67-    (checkColGeFn "indented command sequence" >> rawLineFn))
68-
69-private def rawCommandBlockFn : ParserFn :=
70-  rawFn (rawLineFn >> manyFn rawIndentedLineFn) (trailingWs := true)
71-
72-private def rawCommandBlock : Parser := { fn := rawCommandBlockFn }
73-
74-@[combinator_parenthesizer rawCommandBlock]
75-private def rawCommandBlock.parenthesizer := PrettyPrinter.Parenthesizer.visitToken
76-
77-@[combinator_formatter rawCommandBlock]
78-private def rawCommandBlock.formatter := PrettyPrinter.Formatter.visitAtom Name.anonymous
79-
80-private partial def runRawCmdsAux
81-    (ictx : InputContext) (pstate : ModuleParserState) : CommandElabM Unit := do
82-  let state ← get
83-  let scope := state.scopes.head!
84-  let pctx :=  {
85-      env := state.env
86-      options := scope.opts
87-      currNamespace := scope.currNamespace
88-      openDecls := scope.openDecls : ParserModuleContext
89-    }
90-  let (cmd, pstate, messages) := parseCommand ictx pctx pstate state.messages
91-  modify fun state => { state with messages }
92-  unless cmd.isOfKind ``Command.eoi do
93-    elabCommand cmd
94-    runLinters cmd
95-    unless isTerminalCommand cmd do
96-      runRawCmdsAux ictx pstate
97-
98-/- Recovers the source info and elaborates the commands -/
99-private def runRawCmds (body : Syntax) : CommandElabM Unit := do
100-  let some source := body.getSubstring? (withLeading := false) (withTrailing := false)
101-    | throwErrorAt body "command sequence has no source range"
102-  let fileName ← getFileName
103-  let fileMap ← getFileMap
104-  -- Recall that `rawIndentedLineFn` may consume whitespaces after the newline.
105-  -- Here we move the ending back to the last non-whitespace character to produce
106-  -- correctly positioned diagnostics.
107-  let stopPos := source.trimRight.stopPos
108-  if h : stopPos ≤ fileMap.source.rawEndPos then
109-    let ictx := InputContext.mk fileMap.source fileName
110-      (fileMap := fileMap) (endPos := stopPos) (endPos_valid := h)
111-    runRawCmdsAux ictx { pos := source.startPos, recovering := false, hasLeading := false }
112-  else
113-    throwErrorAt body "invalid command-sequence source range"
114-
115-end IndentedCommands
116-
117-end

3--- # Slang: Arithmetic and Boolean Expressions
4-
5--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
6---     We need to figure out our approach to text width,
7---     especially for proofs. Quite a few proofs here don't
8---     render into the chosen page width, and for terse mode it
9---     will be worse.
10-
11--- ## Arithmetic and Boolean Expressions
12-
13--- ### Syntax
14-
15-namespace Slang
16-
17--- Abstract syntax trees for arithmetic and boolean
18--- expressions:
19-
20-inductive Aexp where
21-  | num (n : Nat)
22-  | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
23-  | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
24-  | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp)
25-
26-inductive Bexp where
27-  | bool (b : Bool)
28-  | eq (a1 a2 : Aexp)
29-  | neq (a1 a2 : Aexp)
30-  | le (a1 a2 : Aexp)
31-  | gt (a1 a2 : Aexp)
32-  | not (b : Bexp)
33-  | and (b1 b2 : Bexp)
34-
35--- ### Evaluation
36-
37--- *Evaluating* an arithmetic expression produces a number.
38-
39-def Aexp.eval (a : Aexp) : Nat :=
40-  match a with
41-  | num   n     =>  n
42-  | plus  a1 a2 =>  a1.eval + a2.eval
43-  | minus a1 a2 =>  a1.eval - a2.eval
44-  | mult  a1 a2 =>  a1.eval * a2.eval
45-
46-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_num (n : Nat) : (num n).eval = n := rfl
47-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_plus (a1 a2 : Aexp) : (plus a1 a2).eval = a1.eval + a2.eval := rfl
48-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_minus (a1 a2 : Aexp) : (minus a1 a2).eval = a1.eval - a2.eval := rfl
49-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_mult (a1 a2 : Aexp) : (mult a1 a2).eval = a1.eval * a2.eval := rfl
50-
51-example : Aexp.eval (.plus (.num 2) (.num 2)) = 4 := by simp
52-
53--- Similarly, evaluating a boolean expression yields a boolean,
54--- and we give it the same treatment.
55-
56-def Bexp.eval (b : Bexp) : Bool :=
57-  match b with
58-  | bool b     =>  b
59-  | eq   a1 a2 =>  a1.eval == a2.eval
60-  | neq  a1 a2 =>  a1.eval != a2.eval
61-  | le   a1 a2 =>  a1.eval ≤ a2.eval
62-  | gt   a1 a2 =>  a1.eval > a2.eval
63-  | not  b1    =>  !eval b1
64-  | and  b1 b2 =>  eval b1 && eval b2
65-
66-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_bool (b : Bool) : (bool b).eval = b := rfl
67-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_eq (a1 a2 : Aexp) : (eq a1 a2).eval = (a1.eval == a2.eval) := rfl
68-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_neq (a1 a2 : Aexp) : (neq a1 a2).eval = (a1.eval != a2.eval) := rfl
69-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_le (a1 a2 : Aexp) : (le a1 a2).eval = (a1.eval ≤ a2.eval : Bool) := rfl
70-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_gt (a1 a2 : Aexp) : (gt a1 a2).eval = (a1.eval > a2.eval : Bool) := rfl
71-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_not (b : Bexp) : (not b).eval = !b.eval := rfl
72-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_and (b1 b2 : Bexp) : (and b1 b2).eval = (b1.eval && b2.eval) := rfl
73-
74--- It's worth noting that `≤` and `>` are `Prop`-valued, i.e.
75--- `a1.eval st ≤ a2.eval st` is a proposition, but `Bexp.eval`
76--- returns a `Bool` so Lean implicitly inserts a `decide`
77--- coercion. You can observe the call to `decide` by hovering
78--- over `Bexp.eval_le` and `Bexp.eval_gt`.
79-
80--- _Quiz:_
81-
82--- What does the following expression evaluate to?
83-
84--- Aexp.eval (.plus (.num 3) (.minus (.num 4) (.num 1)))
85-
86--- (A) true (B) false (C) 0 (D) 3 (E) 6
87-
88--- ### Optimization
89-
90-def Aexp.optimize0plus (a : Aexp) : Aexp :=
91-  match a with
92-  | num   n          => num n
93-  | plus  (num 0) e2 => optimize0plus e2
94-  | plus  e1      e2 => plus  (optimize0plus e1) (optimize0plus e2)
95-  | minus e1      e2 => minus (optimize0plus e1) (optimize0plus e2)
96-  | mult  e1      e2 => mult  (optimize0plus e1) (optimize0plus e2)
97-
98-example :
99-    Aexp.optimize0plus (.plus (.num 2)
100-                               (.plus (.num 0)
101-                                      (.plus (.num 0) (.num 1))))
102-      = .plus (.num 2) (.num 1) := by rfl
103-
104-theorem optimize0plus_sound (a : Aexp) :
105-    a.optimize0plus.eval = a.eval := by
106-  induction a with
107-  | num n => rfl
108-  | plus a1 a2 ih1 ih2 =>
109-    cases a1 with
110-    | num n =>
111-      cases n with
112-      | zero =>
113-        simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus, Aexp.eval_num, Nat.zero_add]
114-        exact ih2
115-      | succ n =>
116-        simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus, Aexp.eval_num]
117-        rw [ih2]
118-    | plus b1 b2 =>
119-      simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus] at ih1 ⊢
120-      rw [ih1, ih2]
121-    | minus b1 b2 =>
122-      simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus] at ih1 ⊢
123-      rw [ih1, ih2]
124-    | mult b1 b2 =>
125-      simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus] at ih1 ⊢
126-      rw [ih1, ih2]
127-  | minus a1 a2 ih1 ih2 =>
128-    simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_minus]
129-    rw [ih1, ih2]
130-  | mult a1 a2 ih1 ih2 =>
131-    simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_mult]
132-    rw [ih1, ih2]
133-
134-theorem optimize0plus_sound' (a : Aexp) :
135-    a.optimize0plus.eval = a.eval := by
136-  fun_induction Aexp.optimize0plus a <;> simp_all
137-
138--- ### Exercise (3 stars): optimize0plusB_sound ⭐⭐⭐
139-
140--- Since the `Aexp.optimize0plus` transformation doesn't change
141--- the value of an `Aexp`, we should be able to apply it to all
142--- the `Aexp`s that appear in a `Bexp` without changing the
143--- `Bexp`'s value. Write a function that performs this
144--- transformation on `Bexp`s and prove it sound. Use the
145--- combinators we've just seen to make the proof as short and
146--- elegant as possible.
147-
148-def Bexp.optimize0plusB (b : Bexp) : Bexp := sorry
149-
150-theorem optimize0plusB_test1 :
151-    Bexp.optimize0plusB
152-        (.not (.gt (.plus (.num 0) (.num 4)) (.num 8)))
153-      = (.not (.gt (.num 4) (.num 8))) := sorry
154-
155-theorem optimize0plusB_test2 :
156-    Bexp.optimize0plusB
157-        (.and (.le (.plus (.num 0) (.num 4)) (.num 5)) (.bool true))
158-      = (.and (.le (.num 4) (.num 5)) (.bool true)) := sorry
159-
160-theorem optimize0plusB_sound (b : Bexp) :
161-    b.optimize0plusB.eval = b.eval := by
162-  sorry

164--- ### Exercise (4 stars): optimize ⭐⭐⭐⭐
165-
166--- The optimization implemented by our `Aexp.optimize0plus` is
167--- only one of many possible optimizations on arithmetic and
168--- boolean expressions. Write a more sophisticated optimizer
169--- and prove it correct. (You will probably find it easiest to
170--- start small -- add just a single, simple optimization and
171--- its correctness proof -- and build up incrementally to
172--- something more interesting.)

174--- ## Evaluation as a Relation
175-
176-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
177-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
178-  | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
179-      EvalR (.plus a1 a2) (n1 + n2)
180-  | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
181-      EvalR (.minus a1 a2) (n1 - n2)
182-  | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
183-      EvalR (.mult a1 a2) (n1 * n2)
184-
185--- One comment on the style of this definition. We could
186--- instead have presented this relation with **positional**
187--- hypotheses -- no names for the premises.
188-
189-namespace ArithUnnamed
190-
191-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
192-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
193-  | plus (e1 e2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) : EvalR e1 n1 → EvalR e2 n2 → EvalR (.plus e1 e2) (n1 + n2)
194-  | minus (e1 e2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) : EvalR e1 n1 → EvalR e2 n2 → EvalR (.minus e1 e2) (n1 - n2)
195-  | mult (e1 e2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) : EvalR e1 n1 → EvalR e2 n2 → EvalR (.mult e1 e2) (n1 * n2)
196-
197-end ArithUnnamed

259-theorem Aexp.evalR_iff_eval (a : Aexp) (n : Nat) :
260-    a ⇓ n ↔ a.eval = n := by
261-  constructor
262-  · intro h
263-    induction h with
264-    | num n => rfl
265-    | plus a1 a2 n1 n2 h1 h2 ih1 ih2 => simp only [Aexp.eval_plus]; rw [ih1, ih2]
266-    | minus a1 a2 n1 n2 h1 h2 ih1 ih2 => simp only [Aexp.eval_minus]; rw [ih1, ih2]
267-    | mult a1 a2 n1 n2 h1 h2 ih1 ih2 => simp only [Aexp.eval_mult]; rw [ih1, ih2]
268-  · intro h
269-    subst h
270-    induction a with
271-    | num n => exact .num n
272-    | plus a1 a2 ih1 ih2 => exact .plus a1 a2 _ _ ih1 ih2
273-    | minus a1 a2 ih1 ih2 => exact .minus a1 a2 _ _ ih1 ih2
274-    | mult a1 a2 ih1 ih2 => exact .mult a1 a2 _ _ ih1 ih2
275-

311--- ### Computational vs. Relational Definitions
312-
313--- Sometimes relational definitions are the only reasonable
314--- option...
315-
316-namespace Slang.AevalRDivision
317-
318--- For example, suppose that we wanted to extend the arithmetic
319--- operations with division:
320-
321-inductive Aexp where
322-  | num (n : Nat)
323-  | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
324-  | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
325-  | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp)
326-  | div (a1 a2 : Aexp)             -- NEW
327-
328--- Extending the definition of `Aexp.eval` to handle this new
329--- operation would not be straightforward due to division being
330--- a *partial* operation; i.e., what should we return as the
331--- result of `.div (.num 5) (.num 0)`? By contrast, partiality
332--- is no problem for the relational version of the definition.
333-
334--- What should `Aexp.eval` return for
335--- `.div (.num 1) (.num 0)`??
336-
337-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
338-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
339-  | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
340-      EvalR (.plus a1 a2) (n1 + n2)
341-  | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
342-      EvalR (.minus a1 a2) (n1 - n2)
343-  | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
344-      EvalR (.mult a1 a2) (n1 * n2)
345-  | div (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 n3 : Nat)             -- NEW
346-      (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) (hpos : n2 > 0) (hdiv : n2 * n3 = n1) :
347-      EvalR (.div a1 a2) n3
348-
349--- Notice that there are some inputs (those with a divisor of
350--- 0) for which this relation does not specify an output.
351-
352-end Slang.AevalRDivision
353-
354-namespace Slang.AevalRExtended
355-
356--- Another example: a *nondeterministic* number generator:
357-
358--- As another example, suppose that we want to extend the
359--- arithmetic operations by a nondeterministic number generator
360--- `any` that, when evaluated, may yield any number. (This is
361--- not the same as making a *probabilistic* choice among all
362--- numbers -- we only say which results are *possible*.)
363-
364-inductive Aexp where
365-  | any                            -- NEW
366-  | num (n : Nat)
367-  | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
368-  | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
369-  | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp)
370-
371--- Again, extending `Aexp.eval` would be tricky, since
372--- evaluation is now *not* a deterministic function from
373--- expressions to numbers; but extending the relation is no
374--- problem.
375-
376--- What should `Aexp.eval` do with nondeterminism??
377-
378-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
379-  | any (n : Nat) : EvalR .any n                   -- NEW
380-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
381-  | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
382-      EvalR (.plus a1 a2) (n1 + n2)
383-  | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
384-      EvalR (.minus a1 a2) (n1 - n2)
385-  | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
386-      EvalR (.mult a1 a2) (n1 * n2)
387-
388-end Slang.AevalRExtended

60--- ## Big-step and Small-step Evaluation
61-
62--- Our semantics for expressions is written in the so-called
63--- "big-step" style. Evaluation rules take an expression to a
64--- final answer "all in one step":
65-
66--- 2 + 2 + 3 * 4 ⇓ 16
67-
68--- But big-step semantics makes it hard to talk about what
69--- happens *along the way*.
70-
71--- *Small-step* style: alternatively, we can show how to
72--- "reduce" an expression to a simpler form by performing a
73--- single step of computation:
74-
75--- 2 + 2 + 3 * 4
76--- ⟶ 2 + 2 + 12
77--- ⟶ 4 + 12
78--- ⟶ 16
79-
80--- Advantages of the small-step style include:
81-
82--- - Finer-grained "abstract machine", closer to real
83---   implementations.
84-
85--- - Extends smoothly to concurrent languages and languages with
86---   other sorts of *computational effects*.
87-
88--- - Separates *divergence* (nontermination) from *stuckness*
89---   (run-time error).
90-
91--- ## A Toy Language
92-
93-inductive Tm where
94-  | c (n : Nat)          -- Constant
95-  | p (t1 t2 : Tm)       -- Plus
96-
97--- A standard big-step evaluator, as a function.

209--- ## Relations
210-
211--- The step relation `⟶` is an example of a relation on `Tm`.
212-
213--- Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1, before next release):
214---     Should we be getting this (and `Deterministic`, `Multi`,
215---     etc. if appropriate) from the Lean standard library? If
216---     not, should we match the concepts in CSLib, if they
217---     exists there?
218-
219-def Relation (X : Type) := X → X → Prop
220-
221--- One simple property a relation may have is being
222--- *deterministic*: like Slang's big-step evaluation, each
223--- element is related to at most one other.
224-
225--- *Theorem*: For each `t`, there is at most one `t'` such that
226--- `t` steps to `t'`. We prove it by induction on the
227--- derivation of the first step.
228-
229--- *Proof sketch*: We show that if `x` steps to both `y1` and
230--- `y2`, then `y1` and `y2` are equal, by induction on a
231--- derivation of `x ⟶ y1`. There are several cases, depending
232--- on the last rule used in this derivation and the last rule
233--- in the given derivation of `x ⟶ y2`.
234-
235--- - If both are `plus`, the result is immediate.
236-
237--- - The cases when both derivations end with `plusLeft` or
238---   `plusRight` follow by the induction hypothesis.
239-
240--- - It cannot happen that one is `plus` and the other is
241---   `plusLeft`/`plusRight`, since this would imply that `x` has
242---   the form `p t1 t2` where both `t1` and `t2` are constants
243---   (by `plus`) *and* one of `t1` or `t2` has the form `p _`.
244-
245--- - Similarly, it cannot happen that one is `plusLeft` and the
246---   other is `plusRight`, since this would imply that `x` has
247---   the form `p t1 t2` where `t1` has both the form `p t11 t12`
248---   and the form `c n`.
249-
250--- Formally,
251-
252-def Deterministic {X : Type} (R : Relation X) : Prop :=
253-  ∀ x y1 y2 : X, R x y1 → R x y2 → y1 = y2
254-
255-namespace SimpleArith2
256-
257-theorem step_deterministic : Deterministic SimpleArith1.Step := by
258-  intro x y1 y2 h1
259-  induction h1 generalizing y2 with
260-  | plus n1 n2 =>
261-      intro h2
262-      cases h2 <;> first | rfl | cases ‹SimpleArith1.Step (.c _) _›
263-  | plusLeft t1 t1' t2 hs ih =>
264-      intro h2
265-      cases h2 <;> first | cases ‹SimpleArith1.Step (.c _) _› | rw [ih _ ‹SimpleArith1.Step t1 _›]
266-  | plusRight n1 t2 t2' hs ih =>
267-      intro h2
268-      cases h2 <;> first | cases ‹SimpleArith1.Step (.c _) _› | rw [ih _ ‹SimpleArith1.Step t2 _›]
269-
270-end SimpleArith2
271-
272--- Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1):
273---     In the Rocq there is the development of a special tactic
274---     to make this proof simpler. Do we want that here?

277-
278--- Final states of our machine are terms of the form `c n`. We
279--- call such terms *values*.
280-
281-inductive IsValue : Tm → Prop where
282-  | const (n : Nat) : IsValue (.c n)

284--- Here are the formal rules.
285-
286-inductive Step : Tm → Tm → Prop where
287-  | plus (n1 n2 : Nat) :
288-      Step (.p (.c n1) (.c n2)) (.c (n1 + n2))
289-  | plusLeft (t1 t1' t2 : Tm)
290-      (h : Step t1 t1') :
291-      Step (.p t1 t2) (.p t1' t2)
292-  | plusRight (v1 t2 t2' : Tm)
293-      (hv : IsValue v1)
294-      (h : Step t2 t2') :
295-      Step (.p v1 t2) (.p v1 t2')
296-
297-notation:40 t:41 " ⟶ " t':41 => Step t t'

301--- As a sanity check on this change, let's re-verify
302--- determinism. Here's an informal proof:
303-
304--- *Proof sketch*: We must show that if `x` steps to both `y1`
305--- and `y2`, then `y1` and `y2` are equal. Consider the final
306--- rules used in the derivations of `x ⟶ y1` and `x ⟶ y2`.
307-
308--- - If both are `plus`, the result is immediate.
309-
310--- - The cases when both derivations end with `plusLeft` or
311---   `plusRight` follow by the induction hypothesis.
312-
313--- - It cannot happen that one is `plus` and the other is
314---   `plusLeft`/`plusRight`, since this would imply that `x` has
315---   the form `p t1 t2` where both `t1` and `t2` are constants
316---   (by `plus`) *and* one of `t1` or `t2` has the form `p _`.
317-
318--- - Similarly, it cannot happen that one is `plusLeft` and the
319---   other is `plusRight`, since this would imply that `x` has
320---   the form `p t1 t2` where `t1` both has the form `p t11 t12`
321---   and is a value (hence has the form `c n`).
322-
323--- Most of this proof is the same as the one above. But to get
324--- maximum benefit from the exercise you should try to write
325--- your formal version from scratch and just use the earlier
326--- one if you get stuck. The impossible cross-cases now also
327--- use the fact that a `IsValue` (a `c n`) cannot step.
328-
329-theorem step_deterministic : Deterministic Step := by
330-  sorry

332--- ### Strong Progress and Normal Forms
333-
334-theorem strong_progress (t : Tm) : IsValue t ∨ ∃ t', t ⟶ t' := by
335-  induction t with
336-  | c n => left; exact .const n
337-  | p t1 t2 ih1 ih2 =>
338-      right
339-      cases ih1 with
340-      | inl hv1 =>
341-          cases ih2 with
342-          | inl hv2 =>
343-              cases hv1 with
344-              | const n1 =>
345-                  cases hv2 with
346-                  | const n2 => exact ⟨.c (n1 + n2), .plus n1 n2⟩
347-          | inr h2 =>
348-              obtain ⟨t2', ht2⟩ := h2
349-              exact ⟨.p t1 t2', .plusRight t1 t2 t2' hv1 ht2⟩
350-      | inr h1 =>
351-          obtain ⟨t1', ht1⟩ := h1
352-          exact ⟨.p t1' t2, .plusLeft t1 t1' t2 ht1⟩
353-
354-def IsNormalForm {X : Type} (R : Relation X) (t : X) : Prop :=
355-  ¬ ∃ t', R t t'
356-
357--- We can use this terminology to generalize the observation we
358--- made in the strong progress theorem: in this language
359--- (though not necessarily, in general), normal forms and
360--- values are actually the same thing.
361-
362-theorem value_is_nf (v : Tm) (h : IsValue v) : IsNormalForm Step v := by
363-  intro hc
364-  obtain ⟨t', ht⟩ := hc
365-  cases h with
366-  | const n => cases ht
367-
368-theorem nf_is_value (t : Tm) (h : IsNormalForm Step t) : IsValue t := by
369-  cases strong_progress t with
370-  | inl hv => exact hv
371-  | inr hstep => exact absurd hstep h
372-
373-theorem nf_same_as_value (t : Tm) : IsNormalForm Step t ↔ IsValue t :=
374-  ⟨nf_is_value t, value_is_nf t⟩
375-
376--- Why is this interesting? Because `IsValue` is a *syntactic*
377--- concept — it is defined by looking at the way a term is
378--- written — while `IsNormalForm` is a *semantic* one — it is
379--- defined by looking at how the term steps.
380-
381--- It is not obvious that these concepts should characterize
382--- the same set of terms!
383-
384--- Indeed, we could easily have written the definitions
385--- (incorrectly) so that they would *not* coincide.
386-
387--- Suppose, for example, we define `IsValue` so that it
388--- includes some terms that are not finished reducing. (Even if
389--- you don't work the exercise `value_not_same_as_normal_form1`
390--- below and the following ones, make sure you can think of an
391--- example of such a term.)
392-
393-namespace Temp1
394-
395-inductive IsValue : Tm → Prop where
396-  | const (n : Nat) : IsValue (.c n)
397-  | funny (t1 : Tm) (n : Nat) : IsValue (.p t1 (.c n))     -- <---
398-
399-inductive Step : Tm → Tm → Prop where
400-  | plus (n1 n2 : Nat) : Step (.p (.c n1) (.c n2)) (.c (n1 + n2))
401-  | plusLeft (t1 t1' t2 : Tm) (h : Step t1 t1') : Step (.p t1 t2) (.p t1' t2)
402-  | plusRight (v1 t2 t2' : Tm) (hv : IsValue v1) (h : Step t2 t2') : Step (.p v1 t2) (.p v1 t2')

497--- ## Multi-Step Reduction
498-
499-inductive Multi {X : Type} (R : Relation X) : X → X → Prop where
500-  | refl (x : X) : Multi R x x
501-  | step (x y z : X) (h1 : R x y) (h2 : Multi R y z) : Multi R x z
502-
503--- Note to developers (berberman):
504---     I would make some arguments implicit to proivde a
505---     cleaner interface (FYI the [mathlib
506---     version](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Logic/Relation.html#Relation.ReflTransGen))
507-
508--- We write `⟶*` for the `Multi Step` relation on terms
509-
510-notation:40 t:41 " ⟶* " t':41 => Multi Step t t'
511-
512--- The relation `Multi R` has several crucial properties.
513-
514-attribute [refl] Multi.refl
515-
516-example : (.c 5 : Tm) ⟶* .c 5 := by rfl
517-
518-example : (.p (.c 1) (.c 2)) ⟶* .c (1 + 2) := by
519-  apply Multi.step (y := .c (1 + 2))
520-  · exact .plus 1 2
521-  · rfl
522-
523-theorem multi_single {X : Type} (R : Relation X) (x y : X) (h : R x y) :
524-    Multi R x y :=
525-  .step x y y h (.refl y)
526-
527-theorem multi_trans {X : Type} (R : Relation X) (x y z : X)
528-    (g : Multi R x y) (h : Multi R y z) : Multi R x z := by
529-  induction g with
530-  | refl a => exact h
531-  | step a b c h1 h2 ih => exact .step a b z h1 (ih h)
532-

534-

536--- expressed as `Multi R` for some `R`?
537-
538--- (A) less than or equal (B) strictly less than (C) equal (D)
539--- none of the above

574--- ### Normal Forms Again
575-
576--- If `t` reduces to `t'` in zero or more steps and `t'` is a
577--- normal form, we say that "`t'` is *a normal form of* `t`."
578-
579-def IsNormalFormOf {X : Type} (R : Relation X) (t t' : X) : Prop :=
580-  Multi R t t' ∧ IsNormalForm R t'
581-
582--- When `R` is deterministic (as for our language's semantics),
583--- then its normal form is *unique*.
584-
585--- ### Exercise (3 stars): normal_forms_unique ⭐⭐⭐
586-
587-theorem normal_forms_unique : Deterministic (IsNormalFormOf Step) := by
588-  -- We recommend using this initial setup as-is!
589-  intro x y1 y2 p1 p2
590-  obtain ⟨p11, p12⟩ := p1
591-  obtain ⟨p21, p22⟩ := p2
592-  sorry
593-
594--- The `Step` relation is *normalizing* it is deterministic and
595--- always reaches a normal form in a finite number of steps.
596-
597-def Normalizing {X : Type} (R : Relation X) : Prop :=
598-  ∀ t, ∃ t', IsNormalFormOf R t t'
599-
600-theorem multistep_congr_1 (t1 t1' t2 : Tm) (h : t1 ⟶* t1') : (.p t1 t2) ⟶* (.p t1' t2) := by
601-  induction h with
602-  | refl x => exact .refl _
603-  | step x y z h1 h2 ih => exact .step _ (.p y t2) _ (.plusLeft x y t2 h1) ih
604-
605--- ### Exercise (2 stars): multistep_congr_2 ⭐⭐
606-
607-theorem multistep_congr_2 (v1 t2 t2' : Tm) (hv : IsValue v1) (h : t2 ⟶* t2') :
608-    (.p v1 t2) ⟶* (.p v1 t2') := by
609-  sorry
610-
611-theorem step_normalizing : Normalizing Step := by
612-  intro t
613-  induction t with
614-  | c n => exact ⟨.c n, .refl _, (nf_same_as_value _).mpr (.const n)⟩
615-  | p t1 t2 ih1 ih2 =>
616-      obtain ⟨t1', hs1, hnf1⟩ := ih1
617-      obtain ⟨t2', hs2, hnf2⟩ := ih2
618-      obtain ⟨n1⟩ := (nf_same_as_value _).mp hnf1
619-      obtain ⟨n2⟩ := (nf_same_as_value _).mp hnf2
620-      apply Exists.intro (.c (n1 + n2))
621-      apply And.intro _ ((nf_same_as_value _).mpr (.const _))
622-      apply multi_trans _ _ _ _ (multistep_congr_1 t1 (.c n1) t2 hs1)
623-      apply multi_trans _ _ _ _ (multistep_congr_2 (.c n1) t2 (.c n2) (.const n1) hs2)
624-      exact multi_single _ _ _ (.plus n1 n2)

626--- ### Equivalence of Big-Step and Small-Step
627-
628--- Having defined the operational semantics of our tiny
629--- programming language in two different ways (big-step and
630--- small-step), it makes sense to ask whether these definitions
631--- actually define the same thing!
632-
633--- They do, though it takes a little work to show it. The
634--- details are left as an exercise. We consider the two
635--- implications separately. First, big-step evaluation implies
636--- multi-step reduction to a value.
637-
638--- ### Exercise (3 stars): multistep_of_eval ⭐⭐⭐
639-
640-theorem multistep_of_eval (t : Tm) (n : Nat) (h : t ⇓ n) : t ⟶* .c n := by
641-  sorry
642-
643--- The key ideas in the proof can be seen in the following
644--- picture:
645-
646--- p t1 t2 ⟶            (by plusLeft)
647--- p t1' t2 ⟶           (by plusLeft)
648--- p t1'' t2 ⟶          (by plusLeft)
649--- ...
650--- p (c n1) t2 ⟶        (by plusRight)
651--- p (c n1) t2' ⟶       (by plusRight)
652--- p (c n1) t2'' ⟶      (by plusRight)
653--- ...
654--- p (c n1) (c n2) ⟶    (by plus)
655--- c (n1 + n2)
656-
657--- That is, the multi-step reduction of a term of the form
658--- `p t1 t2` proceeds in three phases:
659-
660--- - First, we use `plusLeft` some number of times to reduce `t1`
661---   to a normal form, which must (by `nf_same_as_value`) be a
662---   term of the form `c n1` for some `n1`.
663-
664--- - Next, we use `plusRight` some number of times to reduce `t2`
665---   to a normal form, which must again be a term of the form
666---   `c n2` for some `n2`.
667-
668--- - Finally, we use `plus` one time to reduce `p (c n1) (c n2)`
669---   to `c (n1 + n2)`.
670-
671--- To formalize this intuition, you'll need the congruence
672--- lemmas from above, plus some basic properties of `⟶*` (that
673--- it is reflexive, transitive, and includes `⟶`).
674-
675--- ### Exercise (3 stars): multistep_of_eval_inf ⭐⭐⭐
676-
677--- Write a detailed informal version of the proof of
678--- `multistep_of_eval`. (A paper exercise — there is no Lean
679--- proof to fill in here.)
680-
681--- For the converse, we need one lemma, which establishes a
682--- relation between single-step reduction and big-step
683--- evaluation. A single step preserves the big-step value.
684-
685--- ### Exercise (3 stars): eval_of_step ⭐⭐⭐
686-
687-theorem eval_of_step (t t' : Tm) (n : Nat) (hs : t ⟶ t') (he : t' ⇓ n) : t ⇓ n := by
688-  sorry
689-
690--- The fact that small-step reduction implies big-step
691--- evaluation is now straightforward to prove, once we have
692--- factored out the observation that every normal form is a
693--- value. The proof proceeds by induction on the multi-step
694--- reduction sequence that is buried in the hypothesis
695--- `IsNormalFormOf t t'`. (Make sure you understand the
696--- statement before you start to work on the proof.)
697-

699-
700-theorem eval_of_multistep (t t' : Tm) (h : IsNormalFormOf Step t t') :
701-    ∃ n, t' = .c n ∧ t ⇓ n := by
702-  sorry

711--- though!)
712-
713-theorem evalF_eval (t : Tm) (n : Nat) : evalF t = n ↔ t ⇓ n := by

716--- ## Small-Step Slang
717-
718--- Small-step semantics for the richer `Slang` arithmetic and
719--- boolean expressions. Notations: `⟶a` (arithmetic) and `⟶b`
720--- (boolean).
721-
722--- We work in the `Slang` namespace, reusing the arithmetic and
723--- boolean expression syntax (`Aexp`, `Bexp`) and the big-step
724--- evaluator (`Aexp.eval`) from the `Slang` chapter:
725-
726-namespace Slang
727-
728--- ### Arithmetic Expressions
729-
730--- The arithmetic *values* (the normal forms of the small-step
731--- relation below) are just the numeric literals:
732-
733-inductive IsAValue : Aexp → Prop where
734-  | num (n : Nat) : IsAValue (.num n)
735-
736-inductive AStep : Aexp → Aexp → Prop where
737-  | plusLeft (a1 a1' a2 : Aexp) (h : AStep a1 a1') : AStep (.plus a1 a2) (.plus a1' a2)
738-  | plusRight (v1 a2 a2' : Aexp) (hv : IsAValue v1) (h : AStep a2 a2') :
739-      AStep (.plus v1 a2) (.plus v1 a2')
740-  | plus (n1 n2 : Nat) :  AStep (.plus (.num n1) (.num n2)) (.num (n1 + n2))
741-  | minusLeft (a1 a1' a2 : Aexp) (h : AStep a1 a1') : AStep (.minus a1 a2) (.minus a1' a2)
742-  | minusRight (v1 a2 a2' : Aexp) (hv : IsAValue v1) (h : AStep a2 a2') :
743-      AStep (.minus v1 a2) (.minus v1 a2')
744-  | minus (n1 n2 : Nat) : AStep (.minus (.num n1) (.num n2)) (.num (n1 - n2))
745-  | multLeft (a1 a1' a2 : Aexp) (h : AStep a1 a1') : AStep (.mult a1 a2) (.mult a1' a2)
746-  | multRight (v1 a2 a2' : Aexp) (hv : IsAValue v1) (h : AStep a2 a2') :
747-      AStep (.mult v1 a2) (.mult v1 a2')
748-  | mult (n1 n2 : Nat) : AStep (.mult (.num n1) (.num n2)) (.num (n1 * n2))
749-
750-scoped notation:40 a:41 " ⟶a " a':41 => AStep a a'
751-
752--- Here is a one-step reduction: since the left operand `3` is
753--- already a value, the right operand is the one that takes a
754--- step.
755-
756-example :
757-    (Aexp.plus (.num 3) (.plus (.num 2) (.num 1))) ⟶a (.plus (.num 3) (.num 3)) :=
758-  .plusRight _ _ _ (.num 3) (.plus 2 1)

761-
762--- Every arithmetic expression is either a value or can take a
763--- step — the same *strong progress* property we proved for the
764--- toy language, now for the richer `Slang` arithmetic
765--- expressions.
766-
767-theorem strong_progress_arith (a : Aexp) : IsAValue a ∨ ∃ a', a ⟶a a' := by
768-  sorry

770--- ### Boolean Expressions
771-
772-inductive BStep : Bexp → Bexp → Prop where
773-  | eqLeft (a1 a1' a2 : Aexp) (h : AStep a1 a1') : BStep (.eq a1 a2) (.eq a1' a2)
774-  | eqRight (v1 a2 a2' : Aexp) (hv : IsAValue v1) (h : AStep a2 a2') :
775-      BStep (.eq v1 a2) (.eq v1 a2')
776-  | eq (n1 n2 : Nat) : BStep (.eq (.num n1) (.num n2)) (.bool (decide (n1 = n2)))
777-  | neqLeft (a1 a1' a2 : Aexp) (h : AStep a1 a1') : BStep (.neq a1 a2) (.neq a1' a2)
778-  | neqRight (v1 a2 a2' : Aexp) (hv : IsAValue v1) (h : AStep a2 a2') :
779-      BStep (.neq v1 a2) (.neq v1 a2')
780-  | neq (n1 n2 : Nat) : BStep (.neq (.num n1) (.num n2)) (.bool (decide (n1 ≠ n2)))
781-  | leLeft (a1 a1' a2 : Aexp) (h : AStep a1 a1') : BStep (.le a1 a2) (.le a1' a2)
782-  | leRight (v1 a2 a2' : Aexp) (hv : IsAValue v1) (h : AStep a2 a2') :
783-      BStep (.le v1 a2) (.le v1 a2')
784-  | le (n1 n2 : Nat) : BStep (.le (.num n1) (.num n2)) (.bool (decide (n1 ≤ n2)))
785-  | gtLeft (a1 a1' a2 : Aexp) (h : AStep a1 a1') : BStep (.gt a1 a2) (.gt a1' a2)
786-  | gtRight (v1 a2 a2' : Aexp) (hv : IsAValue v1) (h : AStep a2 a2') :
787-      BStep (.gt v1 a2) (.gt v1 a2')
788-  | gt (n1 n2 : Nat) : BStep (.gt (.num n1) (.num n2)) (.bool (decide (n1 > n2)))
789-  | notStep (b1 b1' : Bexp) (h : BStep b1 b1') : BStep (.not b1) (.not b1')
790-  | notTrue : BStep (.not (.bool true)) (.bool false)
791-  | notFalse : BStep (.not (.bool false)) (.bool true)
792-  | andStep (b1 b1' b2 : Bexp) (h : BStep b1 b1') : BStep (.and b1 b2) (.and b1' b2)
793-  | andTrueStep (b2 b2' : Bexp) (h : BStep b2 b2') :
794-      BStep (.and (.bool true) b2) (.and (.bool true) b2')
795-  | andFalse (b2 : Bexp) : BStep (.and (.bool false) b2) (.bool false)
796-  | andTrueTrue : BStep (.and (.bool true) (.bool true)) (.bool true)
797-  | andTrueFalse : BStep (.and (.bool true) (.bool false)) (.bool false)
798-
799-scoped notation:40 b:41 " ⟶b " b':41 => BStep b b'
800-
801--- A boolean example — the left comparison operand reduces
802--- first:
803-
804-example :
805-    (Bexp.le (.plus (.num 1) (.num 1)) (.num 3)) ⟶b (.le (.num 2) (.num 3)) :=
806-  .leLeft _ _ _ (.plus 1 1)
