808--- _Quiz:_
809-
810--- Which of these properties does this small-step semantics for
811--- `Slang` expressions satisfy? (Yes or No for each.)
812-
813--- - determinism
814-
815--- - strong progress (every non-value takes a step)
816-
817--- - values and normal forms coincide (i.e., there are no "stuck"
818---   terms)
819-
820--- - the step relation is normalizing (i.e., evaluation always
821---   terminates)
822-
823--- ### Exercise (3 stars): astep_deterministic ⭐⭐⭐
824-
825--- The arithmetic step relation is deterministic. (Structurally
826--- this is the value-based determinism proof from the toy
827--- language, repeated for `+`, `−`, and `×`; the impossible
828--- cross-cases close because a value `num n` cannot step.)
829-
830-theorem astep_deterministic : Deterministic AStep := by
831-  sorry
832-
833--- ### Exercise (3 stars): bstep_deterministic ⭐⭐⭐
834-
835--- The boolean step relation is deterministic too. The
836--- comparison cases (`eq`, `neq`, `le`, `gt`) reduce their
837--- operands with `⟶a`, so they inherit determinism from
838--- `astep_deterministic`; `¬` and the short-circuiting `∧`
839--- contribute only base cases.
840-
841-theorem bstep_deterministic : Deterministic BStep := by
842-  sorry
843-
844--- ### Nondeterministic Evaluation
845-
846--- `⟶n`: like `⟶a`, but with the `IsAValue` guard on the "step
847--- the right operand" rules removed, so the evaluation order is
848--- nondeterministic.
849-
850-inductive ANStep : Aexp → Aexp → Prop where
851-  | plusLeft (a1 a1' a2 : Aexp) (h : ANStep a1 a1') :  ANStep (.plus a1 a2) (.plus a1' a2)
852-  | plusRight (a1 a2 a2' : Aexp) (h : ANStep a2 a2') : ANStep (.plus a1 a2) (.plus a1 a2')
853-  | plus (n1 n2 : Nat) : ANStep (.plus (.num n1) (.num n2)) (.num (n1 + n2))
854-  | minusLeft (a1 a1' a2 : Aexp) (h : ANStep a1 a1') : ANStep (.minus a1 a2) (.minus a1' a2)
855-  | minusRight (a1 a2 a2' : Aexp) (h : ANStep a2 a2') : ANStep (.minus a1 a2) (.minus a1 a2')
856-  | minus (n1 n2 : Nat) : ANStep (.minus (.num n1) (.num n2)) (.num (n1 - n2))
857-  | multLeft (a1 a1' a2 : Aexp) (h : ANStep a1 a1') : ANStep (.mult a1 a2) (.mult a1' a2)
858-  | multRight (a1 a2 a2' : Aexp) (h : ANStep a2 a2') : ANStep (.mult a1 a2) (.mult a1 a2')
859-  | mult (n1 n2 : Nat) : ANStep (.mult (.num n1) (.num n2)) (.num (n1 * n2))
860-
861-scoped notation:40 a:41 " ⟶n " a':41 => ANStep a a'
862-
863--- Unlike `⟶a`, this relation really is nondeterministic: a
864--- single term can step in two different ways, depending on
865--- which operand we choose to advance.
866-
867-theorem anstep_not_deterministic : ¬ Deterministic ANStep := by
868-  intro hd
869-  have s1 : ANStep (.plus (.plus (.num 1) (.num 1)) (.plus (.num 2) (.num 2)))
870-      (.plus (.num 2) (.plus (.num 2) (.num 2))) :=
871-    .plusLeft _ _ _ (.plus 1 1)
872-  have s2 : ANStep (.plus (.plus (.num 1) (.num 1)) (.plus (.num 2) (.num 2)))
873-      (.plus (.plus (.num 1) (.num 1)) (.num 4)) :=
874-    .plusRight _ _ _ (.plus 2 2)
875-  have heq := hd _ _ _ s1 s2
876-  simp at heq
877-
878--- ### Exercise (2 stars): anstep_preserves_eval ⭐⭐
879-
880--- Prove that one nondeterministic step leaves the big-step
881--- value unchanged. *Hint:* induction on the step derivation;
882--- each case is immediate from `eval` and, where present, the
883--- induction hypothesis.
884-
885-theorem anstep_preserves_eval (a a' : Aexp) (h : a ⟶n a') : a.eval = a'.eval := by
886-  sorry
887-
888--- This lifts to any number of steps by a routine induction on
889--- the multi-step derivation:
890-
891-theorem multi_anstep_preserves_eval (a a' : Aexp) (h : Multi ANStep a a') : a.eval = a'.eval := by
892-  induction h with
893-  | refl x => rfl
894-  | step x y z h1 _ ih => rw [anstep_preserves_eval x y h1]; exact ih
895-
896-theorem astep_imp_anstep (a a' : Aexp) (h : a ⟶a a') : a ⟶n a' := by
897-  induction h with
898-  | plusLeft a1 a1' a2 _ ih => exact .plusLeft a1 a1' a2 ih
899-  | plusRight v1 a2 a2' _ _ ih => exact .plusRight v1 a2 a2' ih
900-  | plus n1 n2 => exact .plus n1 n2
901-  | minusLeft a1 a1' a2 _ ih => exact .minusLeft a1 a1' a2 ih
902-  | minusRight v1 a2 a2' _ _ ih => exact .minusRight v1 a2 a2' ih
903-  | minus n1 n2 => exact .minus n1 n2
904-  | multLeft a1 a1' a2 _ ih => exact .multLeft a1 a1' a2 ih
905-  | multRight v1 a2 a2' _ _ ih => exact .multRight v1 a2 a2' ih
906-  | mult n1 n2 => exact .mult n1 n2
907-
908-theorem multi_astep_imp_anstep (a a' : Aexp) (h : Multi AStep a a') : Multi ANStep a a' := by
909-  induction h with
910-  | refl x => exact .refl x
911-  | step x y z h1 _ ih => exact .step x y z (astep_imp_anstep x y h1) ih
912-
913--- ### Exercise (3 stars): astep_anstep_agree ⭐⭐⭐
914-
915--- Now put the pieces together: prove that the deterministic
916--- and nondeterministic semantics always compute the *same*
917--- final result. That is, if `a` fully reduces to `.num n1`
918--- under `⟶a` and to `.num n2` under `⟶n`, then `n1 = n2`.
919-
920--- *Hint:* both `.num n1` and `.num n2` are reachable by `⟶n`
921--- (use `multi_astep_imp_anstep` for the first), and `⟶n`
922--- preserves `eval`.
923-
924-theorem astep_anstep_agree (a : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat)
925-    (hd : Multi AStep a (.num n1)) (hn : Multi ANStep a (.num n2)) : n1 = n2 := by
926-  sorry
927-
928--- ### A Small-Step Stack Machine
929-
930--- Our last example is a small-step semantics for a *stack
931--- machine* that evaluates arithmetic expressions. The
932--- machine's instructions push a constant or combine the top
933--- two stack entries. The machine's behavior should match the
934--- big-step `Aexp.eval` function defined earlier.
935-
936--- A *program* is a list of instructions, and the *stack* is a
937--- list of numbers.
938-
939-inductive SInstr where
940-  | push (n : Nat)
941-  | plus
942-  | minus
943-  | mult
944-
945-abbrev Stack := List Nat
946-abbrev Prog := List SInstr
947-
948--- The compiler emits code in the postfix order sketched above:
949-
950-def compile : Aexp → Prog
951-  | .num n => [.push n]
952-  | .plus a1 a2 => compile a1 ++ compile a2 ++ [.plus]
953-  | .minus a1 a2 => compile a1 ++ compile a2 ++ [.minus]
954-  | .mult a1 a2 => compile a1 ++ compile a2 ++ [.mult]
955-
956-example : compile (.plus (.num 2) (.num 3)) = [.push 2, .push 3, .plus] := rfl
957-
958--- Now the small-step machine itself: each step consumes the
959--- next instruction and updates the stack.
960-
961-inductive StackStep : Prog × Stack → Prog × Stack → Prop where
962-  | push (p : Prog) (stk : Stack) (n : Nat) : StackStep (.push n :: p, stk) (p, n :: stk)
963-  | plus (p : Prog) (stk : Stack) (n m : Nat) :
964-      StackStep (.plus :: p, n :: m :: stk) (p, (m + n) :: stk)
965-  | minus (p : Prog) (stk : Stack) (n m : Nat) :
966-      StackStep (.minus :: p, n :: m :: stk) (p, (m - n) :: stk)
967-  | mult (p : Prog) (stk : Stack) (n m : Nat) :
968-      StackStep (.mult :: p, n :: m :: stk) (p, (m * n) :: stk)
969-
970--- The machine is deterministic:
971-
972-theorem stack_step_deterministic : Deterministic StackStep := by
973-  intro x y1 y2 h1 h2
974-  cases h1 <;> cases h2 <;> rfl
975-
976--- ### Exercise (3 stars): compiler_is_correct (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐
977-
978--- Prove the compiler correct: running the compiled program
979--- from the empty stack reduces, in some number of steps, to a
980--- stack holding exactly the value of the expression.
981-
982--- *Hint:* this will not go through by a direct induction — the
983--- induction hypothesis is too weak. Prove a more general
984--- statement first, about running `compile a` followed by *any*
985--- leftover program `p`, starting from *any* stack `stk`.
986--- (Reassociating the `++`s with `List.append_assoc`, and
987--- chaining steps with `multi_trans`/`multi_single`, are the
988--- moves you need.)
989-
990-theorem compiler_is_correct (a : Aexp) :
991-    Multi StackStep (compile a, []) ([], [a.eval]) := by
992-  sorry
993-
994-end Slang

TS/Stlc.lean

1-import Lean.PrettyPrinter.Delaborator
2-import Lean.PrettyPrinter.Parenthesizer
3-import LF.Typeclasses
4-import TS.Smallstep
5-
6-import TS.SFLCompat
7-
8--- # Stlc: The Simply Typed Lambda-Calculus
9-
10--- Our job for this chapter: Formalize a small *functional*
11--- language and its type system.
12-
13--- Language: The *simply typed lambda-calculus* (STLC).
14-
15--- - A small subset of Lean's built-in functional language...
16-
17--- - ...but we'll use different concrete syntax (to avoid
18---   confusion, and for consistency with standard treatments)
19-
20--- Main new technical challenges:
21-
22--- - variable binding
23--- - substitution
24-
25--- The STLC lives in the lower-left front corner of the famous
26--- *lambda cube* (also called the *Barendregt Cube*), which
27--- visualizes three sets of features that can be added to its
28--- simple core:
29-
30--- Calculus of Constructions
31---  type operators +--------+
32---                /|       /|
33---               / |      / |
34--- polymorphism +--------+  |
35---              |  |     |  |
36---              |  +-----|--+
37---              | /      | /
38---              |/       |/
39---              +--------+ dependent types
40---            STLC
41-
42--- Moving from bottom to top in the cube corresponds to adding
43--- *polymorphic types* like `∀ α : Type, α → α`. Adding *just*
44--- polymorphism gives us the famous Girard-Reynolds calculus,
45--- System F.
46-
47--- Moving from front to back corresponds to adding *type
48--- operators* like `List`.
49-
50--- Moving from left to right corresponds to adding *dependent
51--- types* like `∀ n, ArrayOfSize n`.
52-
53--- The top right corner on the back, which combines all three
54--- features, is called the *Calculus of Constructions*. First
55--- studied by Coquand and Huet, it forms the foundation of
56--- Lean's logic.
57-
58--- ## Overview
59-
60--- Begin with some set of *base types* (here, just `Bool`)
61-
62--- Add: variables, function abstractions, and applications
63-
64--- Informal concrete syntax of terms `t`:
65-
66--- t ::= x                     (variable)
67---     | λ x : T . t           (abstraction)
68---     | t t                   (application)
69---     | true                  (constant true)
70---     | false                 (constant false)
71---     | if t then t else t    (conditional)
72-
73--- The *types* of the STLC include the base type `Bool` for
74--- boolean values and arrow types for functions.
75-
76--- T ::= Bool
77---     | T → T
78-
79--- Some examples of STLC terms:
80-
81--- `λx:Bool. x`
82-
83--- The identity function for booleans.
84-
85--- `(λx:Bool. x) true`
86-
87--- The identity function for booleans, applied to the boolean
88--- `true`.
89-
90--- `λx:Bool. if x then false else true`
91-
92--- The boolean "not" function.
93-
94--- `λx:Bool. true`
95-
96--- The constant function that takes every (boolean) argument to
97--- `true`.
98-
99--- `λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x`
100-
101--- A two-argument function that takes two booleans and returns
102--- the first one.
103-
104--- `(λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x) false true`
105-
106--- A two-argument function that takes two booleans and returns
107--- the first one, applied to the booleans `false` and `true`.
108-
109--- `λf:Bool → Bool. f (f true)`
110-
111--- A higher-order function that takes a *function* `f` (from
112--- booleans to booleans) as an argument, applies `f` to `true`,
113--- and applies `f` again to the result.
114-
115--- `(λf:Bool → Bool. f (f true)) (λx:Bool. false)`
116-
117--- The same higher-order function, applied to the constantly
118--- `false` function.
119-
120--- Now reconsider our examples, each along with its type:
121-
122--- - `λx:Bool. x` has type `Bool → Bool`
123-
124--- - `(λx:Bool. x) true` has type `Bool`
125-
126--- - `λx:Bool. if x then false else true` has type `Bool → Bool`
127-
128--- - `λx:Bool. true` has type `Bool → Bool`
129-
130--- - `λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x` has type `Bool → Bool → Bool` (i.e.,
131---   `Bool → (Bool → Bool)`)
132-
133--- - `(λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x) false true` has type `Bool`
134-
135--- The last two, higher-order examples are left off the list on
136--- purpose — working out their types is the subject of the
137--- quizzes that follow.
138-
139--- Note that *all* functions are anonymous.
140-
141--- We'll see how to add named function declarations as
142--- "syntactic sugar" in the `MoreStlc` chapter.
143-
144--- _Quiz:_
145-
146--- What is the type of the following term?
147-
148---   λf:Bool → Bool. f (f true)
149-
150--- (A) `Bool → (Bool → Bool)`
151-
152--- (B) `(Bool → Bool) → Bool`
153-
154--- (C) `Bool → Bool`
155-
156--- (D) `Bool`
157-
158--- (E) none of the above
159-
160--- _Quiz:_
161-
162--- How about the type of this one?
163-
164---   (λf:Bool → Bool. f (f true)) (λx:Bool. false)
165-
166--- (A) `Bool → (Bool → Bool)`
167-
168--- (B) `(Bool → Bool) → Bool`
169-
170--- (C) `Bool → Bool`
171-
172--- (D) `Bool`
173-
174--- (E) none of the above
175-
176--- ## Syntax
177-
178--- We next formalize the syntax of the STLC.
179-
180-namespace Stlc
181-
182-open scoped MyGetElem
183-
184--- ### Types
185-
186-inductive Ty where
187-  | bool
188-  | arrow (T₁ T₂ : Ty)
189-
190--- ### Terms
191-
192-inductive Tm where
193-  | var (x : String)
194-  | app (t₁ t₂ : Tm)
195-  | abs (x : String) (T : Ty) (t : Tm)
196-  | tru
197-  | fls
198-  | ite (c t e : Tm)
199-
200--- We need some notation magic to set up the concrete syntax,
201--- as we did in the Types chapter...
202-
203--- Types and terms are both written inside `<{ … }>`; `~e`
204--- escapes to Lean.
205-
206--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: types
207-
208--- The `stlcTy` grammar covers `Bool`, arrows (written `→` or
209--- `->`, associating to the right), parentheses, and `~e`. A
210--- bare identifier other than `Bool` is spliced in as a Lean
211--- term, so a local `T` — or any Lean expression of type `Ty` —
212--- can appear directly inside the brackets.
213-
214--- To extend the grammar, a later chapter adds a `syntax` line
215--- to the category and a matching `macro_rules` case; that is
216--- all it takes to add a new type construct.
217-
218-declare_syntax_cat stlcTy
219-syntax:max "~" term:max : stlcTy
220-syntax:max "(" stlcTy ")" : stlcTy
221-syntax:max ident : stlcTy
222-syntax:50 stlcTy:51 " → " stlcTy:50 : stlcTy
223-syntax:50 stlcTy:51 " -> " stlcTy:50 : stlcTy
224-syntax:max (name := tyBracket) "<{ " stlcTy " }>" : term
225-
226-macro_rules (kind := tyBracket)
227-  | `(<{ ~$T:term }>)    => pure T
228-  | `(<{ ($T:stlcTy) }>) => `(<{ $T:stlcTy }>)
229-  | `(<{ $x:ident }>) =>
230-      match x.getId.toString with
231-      | "Bool" => `(Ty.bool)
232-      | _ => `(($x : Ty))
233-  | `(<{ $T₁:stlcTy → $T₂:stlcTy }>)  => `(Ty.arrow <{ $T₁:stlcTy }> <{ $T₂:stlcTy }>)
234-  | `(<{ $T₁:stlcTy -> $T₂:stlcTy }>) => `(Ty.arrow <{ $T₁:stlcTy }> <{ $T₂:stlcTy }>)
235-
236--- END DETAILS
237-
238--- We'll write types inside of `<{ ... }>` brackets:
239-
240-#check <{ Bool }>
241-#check <{ Bool -> Bool }>
242-#check <{ (Bool -> Bool) -> Bool }>
243-
244--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: terms
245-
246--- Terms are built from variables, application (associating to
247--- the left), abstraction, the two boolean constants, and
248--- conditionals. A binding occurrence — the `x` in
249--- `λ x : T . t` — has a small grammar of its own, `stlcVar`,
250--- and `varStr` turns it into the string that `Tm.abs` stores.
251-
252--- Because types and terms share the brackets, each
253--- `macro_rules` group says which bracket it belongs to
254--- (`kind := tyBracket`, `kind := tmBracket`), and each
255--- antiquote in a nested quotation says which grammar it came
256--- from. A bare identifier is the one genuinely overlapping
257--- case: `Bool` in term position would otherwise quietly become
258--- a variable named `Bool`, so that rule rejects it, which also
259--- settles which grammar a lone `<{ Bool }>` belongs to.
260-
261--- The last production, `[x := s] t`, is the notation for
262--- substitution; we give it its meaning when we define
263--- substitution below. It binds tighter than application, so
264--- `[x:=s] t₁ t₂` is the application of `[x:=s] t₁` to `t₂`,
265--- and a `λ` or `if` body must be parenthesized:
266--- `[x:=s] (λ y : Bool . x)`.
267-
268-declare_syntax_cat stlcVar
269-syntax:max ident : stlcVar
270-syntax:max "~" term:max : stlcVar
271-
272-open Lean in
273-/-- The string named by a variable in binding position. -/
274-def varStr (x : TSyntax `stlcVar) : MacroM Term :=
275-  match x with
276-  | `(stlcVar| $i:ident) => pure (quote i.getId.toString : Term)
277-  | `(stlcVar| ~$e)      => pure e
278-  | _ => Macro.throwUnsupported
279-
280-declare_syntax_cat stlcTm
281-syntax:max "~" term:max : stlcTm
282-syntax:max "(" stlcTm ")" : stlcTm
283-syntax:max ident : stlcTm
284-syntax:75 stlcTm:75 ppSpace stlcTm:76 : stlcTm
285-syntax:50 "λ " stlcVar " : " stlcTy " . " stlcTm:50 : stlcTm
286-syntax:50 "if " stlcTm:51 " then " stlcTm:50 " else " stlcTm:50 : stlcTm
287-syntax:max "[" stlcVar " := " stlcTm "] " stlcTm:max : stlcTm
288-syntax:max (name := tmBracket) "<{ " stlcTm " }>" : term
289-
290-open Lean in
291-macro_rules (kind := tmBracket)
292-  | `(<{ ~$e:term }>)    => pure e
293-  | `(<{ ($t:stlcTm) }>) => `(<{ $t:stlcTm }>)
294-  | `(<{ $x:ident }>) =>
295-      match x.getId.toString with
296-      | "true"  => `(Tm.tru)
297-      | "false" => `(Tm.fls)
298-      | "Bool"  => Macro.throwErrorAt x "`Bool` is a type, not a term"
299-      | _       => `(Tm.var $(quote x.getId.toString))
300-  | `(<{ $t₁:stlcTm $t₂:stlcTm }>) => `(Tm.app <{ $t₁:stlcTm }> <{ $t₂:stlcTm }>)
301-  | `(<{ λ $x : $T . $t }>) => do
302-      `(Tm.abs $(← varStr x) <{ $T:stlcTy }> <{ $t:stlcTm }>)
303-  | `(<{ if $c then $t else $e }>) =>
304-      `(Tm.ite <{ $c:stlcTm }> <{ $t:stlcTm }> <{ $e:stlcTm }>)
305-
306--- END DETAILS
307-
308--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: printing it back
309-
310--- A *delaborator* runs the grammar backwards: it rebuilds the
311--- concrete syntax from a `Ty` or `Tm` value, so that types and
312--- terms appearing in goals and in `#check` output print as
313--- `<{ λ x : Bool . x }>` rather than as a pile of
314--- constructors. (Setting `pp.notation false` turns it off,
315--- revealing the underlying representation.)
316-
317-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Parenthesizer in
318-/-- Re-inserts parentheses in `stlcTy` output according to the grammar's precedences. -/
319-@[category_parenthesizer stlcTy]
320-def stlcTy.parenthesizer : CategoryParenthesizer | prec => do
321-  maybeParenthesize `stlcTy true wrapParens prec <|
322-    parenthesizeCategoryCore `stlcTy prec
323-where
324-  wrapParens (stx : Syntax) : Syntax := Unhygienic.run do
325-    let pstx ← `(stlcTy| ($(⟨stx⟩)))
326-    return pstx.raw.setInfo (SourceInfo.fromRef stx)
327-
328-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Parenthesizer in
329-/-- Re-inserts parentheses in `stlcTm` output according to the grammar's precedences. -/
330-@[category_parenthesizer stlcTm]
331-def stlcTm.parenthesizer : CategoryParenthesizer | prec => do
332-  maybeParenthesize `stlcTm true wrapParens prec <|
333-    parenthesizeCategoryCore `stlcTm prec
334-where
335-  wrapParens (stx : Syntax) : Syntax := Unhygienic.run do
336-    let pstx ← `(stlcTm| ($(⟨stx⟩)))
337-    return pstx.raw.setInfo (SourceInfo.fromRef stx)
338-
339-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
340-/-- Rebuild `stlcTy` concrete syntax from a `Ty` value. -/
341-partial def delabTyInner : DelabM (TSyntax `stlcTy) := do
342-  let stx ←
343-    match_expr ← getExpr with
344-    | Ty.bool => `(stlcTy| $(mkIdent `Bool):ident)
345-    | Ty.arrow _ _ => do
346-        let a ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTyInner
347-        let b ← withAppArg delabTyInner
348-        `(stlcTy| $a → $b)
349-    | _ => do
350-        match ← delab with
351-        | `($i:ident) => `(stlcTy| $i:ident)
352-        | e => `(stlcTy| ~$e)
353-  (⟨·⟩) <$> annotateTermInfo ⟨stx.raw⟩
354-
355-open Lean in
356-/-- Is `s` usable as a bare identifier in the object syntax? -/
357-def isPlainName (s : String) : Bool :=
358-  !s.isEmpty && s != "_" && !s.front.isDigit &&
359-    s.all fun c => c.isAlphanum || c == '_'
360-
361-open Lean in
362-/-- Is `s` usable as a bare variable in `stlcTm` rather than as reserved syntax? -/
363-def isPlainTmVarName (s : String) : Bool :=
364-  isPlainName s && s != "true" && s != "false" && s != "Bool"
365-
366-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
367-/-- Rebuild `stlcVar` concrete syntax from the string in a binding position. -/
368-def delabVarInner : DelabM (TSyntax `stlcVar) := do
369-  match ← delab with
370-  | `($s:str) =>
371-      if isPlainName s.getString then
372-        `(stlcVar| $(mkIdent (Name.mkSimple s.getString)):ident)
373-      else `(stlcVar| ~$s)
374-  | e => `(stlcVar| ~$e)
375-
376-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
377-/-- Rebuild `stlcTm` concrete syntax from a `Tm` value. -/
378-partial def delabTmInner : DelabM (TSyntax `stlcTm) := do
379-  let stx ←
380-    match_expr ← getExpr with
381-    | Tm.tru => `(stlcTm| $(mkIdent `true):ident)
382-    | Tm.fls => `(stlcTm| $(mkIdent `false):ident)
383-    | Tm.var _ => do
384-        let x ← withAppArg delab
385-        match x with
386-        | `($s:str) =>
387-            if isPlainTmVarName s.getString then
388-              `(stlcTm| $(mkIdent (Name.mkSimple s.getString)):ident)
389-            else
390-              let var : Term := mkIdent ``Stlc.Tm.var
391-              `(stlcTm| ~($var $x))
392-        | _ =>
393-            let var : Term := mkIdent ``Stlc.Tm.var
394-            `(stlcTm| ~($var $x))
395-    | Tm.app _ _ => do
396-        let f ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
397-        let a ← withAppArg delabTmInner
398-        `(stlcTm| $f $a)
399-    | Tm.abs _ _ _ => do
400-        let x ← withAppFn <| withAppFn <| withAppArg delabVarInner
401-        let T ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTyInner
402-        let t ← withAppArg delabTmInner
403-        `(stlcTm| λ $x : $T . $t)
404-    | Tm.ite _ _ _ => do
405-        let c ← withAppFn <| withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
406-        let t ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
407-        let e ← withAppArg delabTmInner
408-        `(stlcTm| if $c then $t else $e)
409-    | _ => do
410-        -- `subst` is defined below, so it is matched by name rather than with
411-        -- `match_expr`; a substitution prints in its own bracket notation.
412-        let e ← getExpr
413-        if e.getAppFn.constName? == some `Stlc.subst && e.getAppNumArgs == 3 then
414-          let x ← withAppFn <| withAppFn <| withAppArg delabVarInner
415-          let s ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
416-          let t ← withAppArg delabTmInner
417-          `(stlcTm| [$x := $s] $t)
418-        else
419-          match ← delab with
420-          | `($i:ident) => `(stlcTm| $i:ident)
421-          | e => `(stlcTm| ~$e)
422-  (⟨·⟩) <$> annotateTermInfo ⟨stx.raw⟩
423-
424-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
425-@[delab app.Stlc.Ty.bool, delab app.Stlc.Ty.arrow]
426-def delabTy : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
427-  guard <| match_expr ← getExpr with
428-    | Ty.bool => true | Ty.arrow _ _ => true | _ => false
429-  match ← delabTyInner with
430-  | `(stlcTy| ~$e) => pure e
431-  | e => `(<{ $e:stlcTy }>)
432-
433-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
434-@[delab app.Stlc.Tm.var, delab app.Stlc.Tm.app, delab app.Stlc.Tm.abs,
435-  delab app.Stlc.Tm.tru, delab app.Stlc.Tm.fls, delab app.Stlc.Tm.ite]
436-def delabTm : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
437-  guard <| match_expr ← getExpr with
438-    | Tm.var _ => true | Tm.app _ _ => true | Tm.abs _ _ _ => true
439-    | Tm.tru => true | Tm.fls => true | Tm.ite _ _ _ => true
440-    | _ => false
441-  match ← delabTmInner with
442-  | `(stlcTm| ~($e)) => pure e
443-  | `(stlcTm| ~$e) => pure e
444-  | e => `(<{ $e:stlcTm }>)
445-
446--- END DETAILS
447-
448--- Here are the terms we will use as running examples, written
449--- in the new notation:
450-
451-abbrev idB := <{ λ x : Bool . x }>
452-
453-abbrev idBB := <{ λ x : Bool → Bool . x }>
454-
455-abbrev idBBBB := <{ λ x : (Bool → Bool) → (Bool → Bool) . x }>
456-
457-abbrev k := <{ λ x : Bool . λ y : Bool . x }>
458-
459-abbrev notB := <{ λ x : Bool . if x then false else true }>
460-
461--- Note that an abstraction `λ x : T . t` (formally, `Tm.abs`
462--- applied to `x`, `T`, and `t`) is always annotated with the
463--- type `T` of its parameter, in contrast to Lean (and other
464--- functional languages like ML, Haskell, etc.), which use type
465--- inference to fill in missing annotations. We're not
466--- considering type inference at all here.
467-
468--- ## Operational Semantics
469-
470--- To define the small-step semantics of STLC terms...
471-
472--- - We begin by defining the set of values.
473-
474--- - Next, we define *free variables* and *substitution*. These
475---   are used in the reduction rule for application expressions.
476-
477--- - Finally, we give the small-step relation itself.
478-
479--- ### Values
480-
481--- To define the values of the STLC, we have a few cases to
482--- consider.
483-
484--- First, for the boolean part of the language, the situation
485--- is clear: `true` and `false` are the only values. An `if`
486--- expression is never a value.
487-
488--- Second, an application is not a value: it represents a
489--- function being invoked on some argument, which clearly still
490--- has work left to do.
491-
492--- Third, for abstractions, we have a choice:
493-
494--- - We can say that `λx:T. t` is a value only when `t` is a
495---   value — i.e., only if the function's body has been reduced
496---   (as much as it can be without knowing what argument it is
497---   going to be applied to).
498-
499--- - Or we can say that `λx:T. t` is always a value, no matter
500---   whether `t` is one or not — in other words, we can say that
501---   reduction stops at abstractions.
502-
503--- Our usual way of evaluating expressions in Lean makes the
504--- first choice — for example,
505-
506-#reduce fun _x : Bool => 3 + 4
507-
508--- yields:
509-
510---   fun _x => 7
511-
512--- But Lean is rather unusual in this respect. Most functional
513--- programming languages make the second choice — reduction of
514--- a function's body only begins when the function is actually
515--- applied to an argument.
516-
517--- We also make the second choice here.
518-
519-inductive Tm.IsValue : Tm → Prop where
520-  | abs (x : String) (T₂ : Ty) (t₁ : Tm) : Tm.IsValue <{ λ ~x : ~T₂ . ~t₁ }>
521-  | tru : Tm.IsValue <{ true }>
522-  | fls : Tm.IsValue <{ false }>
523-
524-theorem idB_value : idB.IsValue := .abs ..
525-theorem idBB_value : idBB.IsValue := .abs ..
526-theorem notB_value : notB.IsValue := .abs ..
527-
528--- Note to developers:
529---     The Rocq source follows each inductive definition in
530---     this chapter with a `Hint Constructors … : core`,
531---     registering the constructors with `auto`; the proofs
532---     then lean on `auto`/`eauto` to assemble derivations. We
533---     have no counterpart here: the proofs below name their
534---     constructors explicitly, in the style of the Types
535---     chapter. Lean's `grind` would be the closest analogue if
536---     a later pass wants automation.
537-
538--- ### STLC Programs
539-
540--- Finally, we must consider what constitutes a *complete*
541--- program.
542-
543--- Intuitively, a "complete program" must not refer to any
544--- undefined variables. We'll see shortly how to define the
545--- *free* variables in a STLC term. A complete program, then,
546--- is one that is *closed* — that is, that contains no free
547--- variables.
548-
549--- (Conversely, a term that may contain free variables is often
550--- called an *open term*.)
551-
552--- Note to developers (Chris Henson @chenson2018, before next release):
553---     Is the "shortly" above setting wrong expectations? Where
554---     exactly are we defining the free variables in a STLC
555---     term? BCP 25: Indeed, we need to define "free"!
556-
557--- Having made the choice not to reduce under abstractions, we
558--- don't need to worry about whether variables are values,
559--- since we'll always be reducing programs "from the outside
560--- in," and that means the `step` relation will always be
561--- working with closed terms.
562-
563--- ### Substitution
564-
565--- Now we come to the heart of the STLC: the operation of
566--- *substituting* one term for a variable in another term. This
567--- operation is used below to define the operational semantics
568--- of function application, where we will need to substitute
569--- the argument term for the function parameter in the
570--- function's body. For example, we reduce
571-
572---   (λx:Bool. if x then true else x) false
573-
574--- to
575-
576---   if false then true else false
577-
578--- by substituting `false` for the parameter `x` in the body of
579--- the function.
580-
581--- In general, we need to be able to substitute some given term
582--- `s` for occurrences of some variable `x` in another term
583--- `t`. Informally, this is written `[x:=s]t` and pronounced
584--- "substitute `s` for `x` in `t`."
585-
586--- Here are some examples:
587-
588--- - `[x:=true] (if x then true else false)` yields
589---   `if true then true else false`
590-
591--- - `[x:=true] x` yields `true`
592-
593--- - `[x:=true] (if x then x else y)` yields
594---   `if true then true else y`
595-
596--- - `[x:=true] y` yields `y`
597-
598--- - `[x:=true] false` yields `false` (vacuous substitution)
599-
600--- - `[x:=true] (λy:Bool. if y then x else false)` yields
601---   `λy:Bool. if y then true else false`
602-
603--- - `[x:=true] (λy:Bool. x)` yields `λy:Bool. true`
604-
605--- - `[x:=true] (λy:Bool. y)` yields `λy:Bool. y`
606-
607--- - `[x:=true] (λx:Bool. x)` yields `λx:Bool. x`
608-
609--- The last example is illuminating: substituting `x` with
610--- `true` in `λx:Bool. x` does *not* yield `λx:Bool. true`! The
611--- reason for this is that the `x` in the body of `λx:Bool. x`
612--- is *bound* by the abstraction: it is a new, local name that
613--- just happens to be spelled the same as some global name `x`.
614-
615--- Here is the definition, informally...
616-
617---   [x:=s]x               = s
618---   [x:=s]y               = y                     if x ≠ y
619---   [x:=s](λx:T. t)       = λx:T. t
620---   [x:=s](λy:T. t)       = λy:T. [x:=s]t         if x ≠ y
621---   [x:=s](t₁ t₂)         = ([x:=s]t₁) ([x:=s]t₂)
622---   [x:=s]true            = true
623---   [x:=s]false           = false
624---   [x:=s](if t₁ then t₂ else t₃) =
625---                   if [x:=s]t₁ then [x:=s]t₂ else [x:=s]t₃
626-
627--- ... and formally:
628-
629-section
630-set_option hygiene false in
631-local macro_rules (kind := tmBracket)
632-  | `(<{ [$x := $s] $t }>) => do
633-      `(subst $(← varStr x) <{ $s:stlcTm }> <{ $t:stlcTm }>)
634-
635-def subst (x : String) (s : Tm) (t : Tm) : Tm :=
636-  match t with
637-  -- `.var y`, not `<{ ~y }>`: `y` is the variable's *name*, a `String`
638-  -- (see the note below the definition).
639-  | .var y =>
640-      if x = y then s else t
641-  | <{ λ ~y : ~T . ~t₁ }> =>
642-      if x = y then t else <{ λ ~y : ~T . [~x := ~s] ~t₁ }>
643-  | <{ ~t₁ ~t₂ }> =>
644-      <{ ([~x := ~s] ~t₁) ([~x := ~s] ~t₂) }>
645-  | <{ true }> =>
646-      <{ true }>
647-  | <{ false }> =>
648-      <{ false }>
649-  | <{ if ~t₁ then ~t₂ else ~t₃ }> =>
650-      <{ if [~x := ~s] ~t₁ then [~x := ~s] ~t₂ else [~x := ~s] ~t₃ }>
651-end
652-
653-macro_rules (kind := tmBracket)
654-  | `(<{ [$x := $s] $t }>) => do
655-      `(subst $(← varStr x) <{ $s:stlcTm }> <{ $t:stlcTm }>)
656-
657--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: substitution
658-
659--- One more line registers substitutions with the printer, so
660--- that a goal mentioning one reads as `[x := s] t` rather than
661--- as a `subst` application.
662-
663-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
664-@[delab app.Stlc.subst]
665-def delabSubst : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
666-  match ← delabTmInner with
667-  | `(stlcTm| ~$e) => pure e
668-  | e => `(<{ $e:stlcTm }>)
669-
670--- END DETAILS
671-
672-variable (x y : String) (s t t₁ t₂ t₃ : Tm) (T : Ty)
673-
674-@[simp] theorem subst_var_eq : <{ [~x := ~s] ~(Tm.var x) }> = s := by
675-  simp [subst]
676-
677-@[simp] theorem subst_var_ne (h : x ≠ y) : <{ [~x := ~s] ~(Tm.var y) }> = .var y := by
678-  simp [subst, h]
679-
680-@[simp] theorem subst_abs_eq : <{ [~x := ~s] (λ ~x : ~T . ~t) }> = <{ λ ~x : ~T . ~t }> := by
681-  simp [subst]
682-
683-@[simp] theorem subst_abs_ne (h : x ≠ y) :
684-    <{ [~x := ~s] (λ ~y : ~T . ~t) }> = <{ λ ~y : ~T . [~x := ~s] ~t }> := by
685-  simp [subst, h]
686-
687-@[simp] theorem subst_app :
688-    <{ [~x := ~s] (~t₁ ~t₂) }> = <{ ([~x := ~s] ~t₁) ([~x := ~s] ~t₂) }> := rfl
689-
690-@[simp] theorem subst_tru : <{ [~x := ~s] true }> = <{ true }> := rfl
691-
692-@[simp] theorem subst_fls : <{ [~x := ~s] false }> = <{ false }> := rfl
693-
694-@[simp] theorem subst_ite :
695-    <{ [~x := ~s] (if ~t₁ then ~t₂ else ~t₃) }> =
696-      <{ if [~x := ~s] ~t₁ then [~x := ~s] ~t₂ else [~x := ~s] ~t₃ }> := rfl
697-
698--- _Quiz:_
699-
700--- What is the result of the following substitution?
701-
702---   [x:=s](λy:T₁. x (λx:T₂. x))
703-
704--- (1) `(λy:T₁. x (λx:T₂. x))`
705-
706--- (2) `(λy:T₁. s (λx:T₂. s))`
707-
708--- (3) `(λy:T₁. s (λx:T₂. x))`
709-
710--- (4) none of the above
711-
712--- *Technical note*: Substitution becomes trickier to define if
713--- we consider the case where `s`, the term being substituted
714--- for a variable in some other term, may itself contain free
715--- variables. We say that `s` is an *open* term.
716-
717--- Here is an example. Using the above definition to substitute
718--- the open term
719-
720---   s = λx:Bool. r
721-
722--- (where `r` is a *free* reference to some global resource)
723--- for the free variable `z` in the term
724-
725---   t = λr:Bool. z
726-
727--- where `r` is a bound variable, we would get
728-
729---   λr:Bool. λx:Bool. r
730-
731--- where the free reference to `r` in `s` has been "captured"
732--- by the binder at the beginning of `t`.
733-
734--- Why would this be bad? Because it violates the principle
735--- that the names of bound variables do not matter. For
736--- example, if we rename the bound variable in `t`, e.g., let
737-
738---   t' = λw:Bool. z
739-
740--- then `[z:=s]t'` is
741-
742---   λw:Bool. λx:Bool. r
743-
744--- which does not behave the same as the substituting in the
745--- original `t`:
746-
747---   [z:=s]t = λr:Bool. λx:Bool. r
748-
749--- That is, renaming a bound variable in `t` would change how
750--- `t` behaves under our simple substitution. So substitution
751--- gets more complicated in that setting, but fortunately we
752--- don't have that problem in our STLC variant.
753-
754--- Fortunately, since we are only interested here in defining
755--- the `step` relation on *closed* terms (i.e., terms like
756--- `λx:Bool. x` that include binders for all of the variables
757--- they mention), we can sidestep this extra complexity, but it
758--- must be dealt with when formalizing richer languages.
759-
760--- ### Reduction
761-
762--- v.IsValue
763---                        -----------------------      (appAbs)
764---                         (λx:T. t) v ⟶ [x:=v]t
765-
766---                               t₁ ⟶ t₁'
767---                           ----------------          (app1)
768---                            t₁ t₂ ⟶ t₁' t₂
769-
770---                               v.IsValue
771---                               t₂ ⟶ t₂'
772---                           ----------------          (app2)
773---                            v₁ t₂ ⟶ v₁ t₂'
774-
775--- (plus the usual rules for conditionals).
776-
777--- The `appAbs` rule is often called *beta-reduction*.
778-
779--- This is *call by value* reduction: to reduce an application
780--- `(t₁ t₂)`, we
781-
782--- - first reduce `t₁` to a value: a function `λx:T. t`
783-
784--- - then reduce the argument `t₂` to a value `v`
785-
786--- - then reduce the application itself by substituting `v` for
787---   the bound variable `x` in the body `t`.
788-
789-section
790-set_option hygiene false in
791-local notation:40 t:41 " ⟶ " t':41 => Step t t'
792-
793-inductive Step : Tm → Tm → Prop where
794-  | appAbs (x : String) (T : Ty) (t v : Tm) (hv : v.IsValue) :
795-      <{ (λ ~x : ~T . ~t) ~v }> ⟶ <{ [~x := ~v] ~t }>
796-  | app1 (t₁ t₁' t₂ : Tm) (h : t₁ ⟶ t₁') :
797-      <{ ~t₁ ~t₂ }> ⟶ <{ ~t₁' ~t₂ }>
798-  | app2 (v₁ t₂ t₂' : Tm) (hv : v₁.IsValue) (h : t₂ ⟶ t₂') :
799-      <{ ~v₁ ~t₂ }> ⟶ <{ ~v₁ ~t₂' }>
800-  | ifTrue (t₁ t₂ : Tm) :
801-      <{ if true then ~t₁ else ~t₂ }> ⟶ t₁
802-  | ifFalse (t₁ t₂ : Tm) :
803-      <{ if false then ~t₁ else ~t₂ }> ⟶ t₂
804-  | ifStep (t₁ t₁' t₂ t₃ : Tm) (h : t₁ ⟶ t₁') :
805-      <{ if ~t₁ then ~t₂ else ~t₃ }> ⟶ <{ if ~t₁' then ~t₂ else ~t₃ }>
806-end
807-
808-scoped notation:40 t:41 " ⟶ " t':41 => Step t t'
809-scoped notation:40 t:41 " ⟶* " t':41 => Multi Step t t'

880--- Example:
881-
882---   (λx:Bool → Bool. x) (λx:Bool. x) ⟶* λx:Bool. x
883-
884--- i.e.,
885-
886---   idBB idB ⟶* idB
887-
888-example : <{ ~idBB ~idB }> ⟶* idB := by
889-  apply Multi.step (y := idB)
890-  · exact .appAbs "x" <{ Bool → Bool }> <{ x }> idB idB_value
891-  · rfl
892-
893--- Example:
894-
895---   (λx:Bool → Bool. x) ((λx:Bool → Bool. x) (λx:Bool. x))
896---         ⟶* λx:Bool. x
897-
898--- i.e.,
899-
900---   (idBB (idBB idB)) ⟶* idB.
901-
902-example : <{ ~idBB (~idBB ~idB) }> ⟶* idB := by
903-  -- the same reduction happens twice, so we name it
904-  have step₁ : <{ ~idBB ~idB }> ⟶ idB := by
905-    exact .appAbs "x" <{ Bool → Bool }> <{ x }> idB idB_value
906-  apply Multi.step (y := <{ ~idBB ~idB }>)
907-  · exact .app2 idBB <{ ~idBB ~idB }> idB idBB_value step₁
908-  apply Multi.step (y := idB)
909-  · exact step₁
910-  · rfl

913-
914---   (λx:Bool → Bool. x)
915---      (λx:Bool. if x then false else true)
916---      true
917---         ⟶* false
918-
919--- i.e.,
920-
921---   (idBB notB) true ⟶* false.

923-example : <{ ~idBB ~notB true }> ⟶* <{ false }> := by
924-  apply Multi.step (y := <{ ~notB true }>)
925-  · exact .app1 <{ ~idBB ~notB }> notB <{ true }>
926-      (.appAbs "x" <{ Bool → Bool }> <{ x }> notB notB_value)
927-  apply Multi.step (y := <{ if true then false else true }>)
928-  · exact .appAbs "x" <{ Bool }> <{ if x then false else true }> <{ true }> .tru
929-  apply Multi.step (y := <{ false }>)
930-  · exact .ifTrue <{ false }> <{ true }>
931-  · rfl

950-  apply Multi.step (y := <{ ~idBB false }>)

952-      (.ifTrue <{ false }> <{ true }>)

966--- ## Typing
967-
968--- Next we consider the typing relation of the STLC, which is
969--- meant to prevent reduction from getting stuck.
970-
971--- ### Contexts
972-
973--- Note to developers (Chris Henson @chenson2018, before next release):
974---     I find the FULL explanation above much better than the
975---     TERSE one below, since the question below seems
976---     ill-posed without extra context. Why would one want to
977---     type a term `x y` if we've just said that we will just
978---     look at closed terms as our programs?
979-
980--- *Question*: What is the type of the term "`x y`"?
981-
982--- *Answer*: It depends on the types of `x` and `y`!
983-
984--- I.e., in order to assign a type to a term, we need to know
985--- what assumptions we should make about the types of its free
986--- variables.
987-
988--- This leads us to a three-place *typing judgment*, informally
989--- written `Γ ⊢ t ⦂ T`, where `Γ` is a "typing context" — a
990--- mapping from variables to their types.
991-
992-abbrev Context := PartialMap String Ty
993-
994--- Following the usual notation for partial maps, we write
995--- `(x ↦ T, Γ)` for "update the partial function `Γ` so that it
996--- maps `x` to `T`."
997-
998--- ### Typing Relation
999-
1000--- Γ x = T₁
1001---                             ------------                       (var)
1002---                              Γ ⊢ x ⦂ T₁
1003-
1004---                         x ↦ T₂ ; Γ ⊢ t₁ ⦂ T₁
1005---                       -------------------------                (abs)
1006---                        Γ ⊢ λx:T₂. t₁ ⦂ T₂ → T₁
1007-
1008---                           Γ ⊢ t₁ ⦂ T₂ → T₁
1009---                             Γ ⊢ t₂ ⦂ T₂
1010---                          ------------------                    (app)
1011---                            Γ ⊢ t₁ t₂ ⦂ T₁
1012-
1013---                           -----------------                    (tru)
1014---                            Γ ⊢ true ⦂ Bool
1015-
1016---                          ------------------                    (fls)
1017---                           Γ ⊢ false ⦂ Bool
1018-
1019---              Γ ⊢ t₁ ⦂ Bool    Γ ⊢ t₂ ⦂ T₁    Γ ⊢ t₃ ⦂ T₁
1020---             ---------------------------------------------      (ite)
1021---                    Γ ⊢ if t₁ then t₂ else t₃ ⦂ T₁
1022-
1023--- We can read the three-place relation `Γ ⊢ t ⦂ T` as: "under
1024--- the assumptions in Γ, the term `t` has the type `T`."
1025-
1026--- In the formal development, we write this judgment inside the
1027--- same `<{ .. }>` brackets.
1028-
1029--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: contexts and judgments
1030-
1031--- Contexts get a grammar of their own, `stlcCtx`. The
1032--- **meaning** is the map update we already have — `x ↦ T ; Γ`
1033--- expands to exactly the `Typeclasses` chapter's partial-map
1034--- update on `Γ` — but its surface syntax has to be our own,
1035--- because inside these brackets all three positions are in
1036--- object syntax. Writing the map notation directly would mean
1037--- writing the binding as `"x" →ₚ <{ Bool → Bool }> ; Γ`: the
1038--- name quoted, and the type escaped back out of the brackets
1039--- it belongs in. The grammar hides those two encoding details,
1040--- and nothing else.
1041-
1042-declare_syntax_cat stlcCtx
1043-syntax:max "∅" : stlcCtx
1044-syntax:max "~" term:max : stlcCtx
1045-syntax:max stlcVar " ↦ " stlcTy " ; " stlcCtx : stlcCtx
1046-
1047-syntax:max (name := judgeBracket) "<{ " stlcCtx " ⊢ " stlcTm " ⦂ " stlcTy " }>" : term
1048-
1049-open Lean in
1050-/-- The `Context` denoted by a context expression. -/
1051-partial def ctxTerm (G : TSyntax `stlcCtx) : MacroM Term :=
1052-  match G with
1053-  | `(stlcCtx| ∅)   => `((∅ : Context))
1054-  | `(stlcCtx| ~$e) => pure e
1055-  | `(stlcCtx| $x:stlcVar ↦ $T:stlcTy ; $G:stlcCtx) => do
1056-      `(PartialMap.update $(← ctxTerm G) $(← varStr x) <{ $T:stlcTy }>)
1057-  | _ => Macro.throwUnsupported
1058-
1059--- As with `subst`, the judgment notation is used inside the
1060--- definition it names, so it is introduced in two steps: the
1061--- rule below is declared `local` with hygiene off, so the
1062--- `HasType` in its expansion resolves to the relation being
1063--- declared, and after the `section` closes it is declared
1064--- again for real use.
1065-
1066-section
1067-set_option hygiene false in
1068-local macro_rules (kind := judgeBracket)
1069-  | `(<{ $G:stlcCtx ⊢ $t:stlcTm ⦂ $T:stlcTy }>) => do
1070-      `(HasType $(← ctxTerm G) <{ $t:stlcTm }> <{ $T:stlcTy }>)
1071-
1072--- END DETAILS
1073-
1074-inductive HasType : Context → Tm → Ty → Prop where
1075-  | var (Γ : Context) (x : String) (T₁ : Ty) (h : Γ[x] = some T₁) :
1076-      <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~(Tm.var x) ⦂ ~T₁ }>
1077-  | abs (Γ : Context) (x : String) (T₁ T₂ : Ty) (t₁ : Tm)
1078-      (h : <{ ~x ↦ ~T₂ ; ~Γ ⊢ ~t₁ ⦂ ~T₁ }>) :
1079-      <{ ~Γ ⊢ λ ~x : ~T₂ . ~t₁ ⦂ ~T₂ → ~T₁ }>
1080-  | app (Γ : Context) (T₁ T₂ : Ty) (t₁ t₂ : Tm)
1081-      (h₁ : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₁ ⦂ ~T₂ → ~T₁ }>) (h₂ : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₂ ⦂ ~T₂ }>) :
1082-      <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₁ ~t₂ ⦂ ~T₁ }>
1083-  | tru (Γ : Context) :
1084-      <{ ~Γ ⊢ true ⦂ Bool }>
1085-  | fls (Γ : Context) :
1086-      <{ ~Γ ⊢ false ⦂ Bool }>
1087-  | ite (Γ : Context) (t₁ t₂ t₃ : Tm) (T₁ : Ty)
1088-      (h₁ : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₁ ⦂ Bool }>) (h₂ : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₂ ⦂ ~T₁ }>)
1089-      (h₃ : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₃ ⦂ ~T₁ }>) :
1090-      <{ ~Γ ⊢ if ~t₁ then ~t₂ else ~t₃ ⦂ ~T₁ }>
1091-
1092--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: the judgment, for real
1093-
1094--- Closing the `section` retires the hygiene-free rule; the
1095--- same rule is then declared again, hygienically, for every
1096--- later use.
1097-
1098-end
1099-
1100-macro_rules (kind := judgeBracket)
1101-  | `(<{ $G:stlcCtx ⊢ $t:stlcTm ⦂ $T:stlcTy }>) => do
1102-      `(HasType $(← ctxTerm G) <{ $t:stlcTm }> <{ $T:stlcTy }>)
1103-
1104--- END DETAILS

1107-
1108--- As with terms, a judgment prints back in its own notation,
1109--- so that a goal reads as `<{ x ↦ Bool ; ∅ ⊢ x ⦂ Bool }>`
1110--- rather than as a `HasType` applied to a chain of map
1111--- updates.

1113-open Lean PrettyPrinter in
1114-/-- Rebuild `stlcCtx` syntax from the term syntax of a `Context`, so that a
1115-context prints as `x ↦ Bool ; Γ` rather than as a chain of map updates. -/
1116-partial def unexpandCtx : Term → UnexpandM (TSyntax `stlcCtx)
1117-  | `(∅) => `(stlcCtx| ∅)
1118-  | `($x:str →ₚ $T) => do
1119-      unexpandCtx (← `($x →ₚ $T ; ∅))
1120-  | `($x:str →ₚ $T ; $G) => do
1121-      let G' ← unexpandCtx G
1122-      let x' : TSyntax `stlcVar ←
1123-        if isPlainName x.getString then
1124-          `(stlcVar| $(mkIdent (Name.mkSimple x.getString)):ident)
1125-        else `(stlcVar| ~$x)
1126-      match T with
1127-      | `(<{ $T':stlcTy }>) => `(stlcCtx| $x':stlcVar ↦ $T' ; $G')
1128-      | _                   => `(stlcCtx| $x':stlcVar ↦ ~($T) ; $G')
1129-  | G => `(stlcCtx| ~($G))
1130-
1131-open Lean PrettyPrinter in
1132-@[app_unexpander Stlc.HasType]
1133-def HasType.unexpand : Unexpander
1134-  | `($_ $G <{ $t:stlcTm }> <{ $T:stlcTy }>) =>
1135-      do `(<{ $(← unexpandCtx G) ⊢ $t ⦂ $T }>)
1136-  | `($_ $G <{ $t:stlcTm }> $T) =>
1137-      do `(<{ $(← unexpandCtx G) ⊢ $t ⦂ ~($T) }>)
1138-  | `($_ $G $t <{ $T:stlcTy }>) =>
1139-      do `(<{ $(← unexpandCtx G) ⊢ ~($t) ⦂ $T }>)
1140-  | `($_ $G $t $T) =>
1141-      do `(<{ $(← unexpandCtx G) ⊢ ~($t) ⦂ ~($T) }>)
1142-  | _ => throw ()
1143-

1146--- ### Examples
1147-
1148-example : <{ ∅ ⊢ λ x : Bool . x ⦂ Bool → Bool }> :=
1149-  .abs _ "x" _ _ _ (.var _ "x" _ rfl)
1150-
1151--- The derivation is small enough to write out directly: an
1152--- abstraction rule whose premise is the variable rule, and the
1153--- variable rule's premise — that the extended context maps `x`
1154--- to `Bool` — holds by computation, hence `rfl`.
1155-
1156--- Note to developers:
1157---     The Rocq source proves this one, and the next, by
1158---     `eauto`, having registered the `has_type` constructors
1159---     in the `core` hint database; it also observes that plain
1160---     `auto` suffices here because the term contains no
1161---     application nodes. We have no hint database, so both
1162---     derivations are given explicitly.
1163-
1164--- More examples:
1165-
1166---   ∅ ⊢ λx:Bool. λy:Bool → Bool. y (y x)
1167---         ⦂ Bool → (Bool → Bool) → Bool.
1168-
1169-example :
1170-    <{ ∅ ⊢ λ x : Bool . λ y : Bool → Bool . y (y x) ⦂
1171-       Bool → (Bool → Bool) → Bool }> :=
1172-  .abs _ _ _ _ _ (.abs _ _ _ _ _
1173-    (.app _ _ Ty.bool _ _ (.var _ "y" _ rfl)
1174-      (.app _ _ Ty.bool _ _ (.var _ "y" _ rfl) (.var _ "x" _ rfl))))
1175-
1176--- We can also show that some terms are *not* typable. For
1177--- example, we can check that there is no typing derivation
1178--- assigning a type to the term `λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x y` — i.e.,
1179-
1180---   ¬ ∃ T, ∅ ⊢ λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x y ⦂ T
1181-
1182-example : ¬ ∃ T, <{ ∅ ⊢ λ x : Bool . λ y : Bool . x y ⦂ ~T }> := by
1183-  intro ⟨T, hc⟩
1184-  -- Each `cases` peels off one rule of the derivation, naming the premise it
1185-  -- leaves behind; the context stays small because the old hypothesis goes away.
1186-  cases hc with
1187-  | abs _ _ _ _ _ h₁ =>
1188-    cases h₁ with
1189-    | abs _ _ _ _ _ h₂ =>
1190-      cases h₂ with
1191-      | app _ _ _ _ _ hf _ =>
1192-        cases hf with
1193-        | var _ _ _ hx =>
1194-          -- `x` is bound to `Bool` in the context, but the application rule
1195-          -- needs it to have an arrow type.
1196-          exact Ty.noConfusion (Option.some.inj hx)
1197-
1198--- Another nonexample:
1199-
1200---   ¬ ∃ S T, ∅ ⊢ λx:S. x x ⦂ T
1201-
1202--- Note to developers:
1203---     The Rocq proof gets to the same contradiction through a
1204---     chain of `inversion`s and then an induction on the
1205---     offending type; the `LATER` note there asks why
1206---     `eauto 30` makes no progress on the previous example,
1207---     and a `NOTATION` note from Ori reports an error with the
1208---     associativity of the arrow in one of the inversion
1209---     hypotheses. Neither issue arises in this encoding.

1232--- (C) `∃ S U T, x ↦ S ; y ↦ U ; ∅ ⊢ λz:Bool. x (y z) ⦂ T`
1233-
1234--- (D) `∃ S T, x ↦ S ; ∅ ⊢ λy:Bool. x (x y) ⦂ T`
1235-
1236-end Stlc

7--- # Types: Type Systems
8-
9--- Note to developers:
10---     LATER: For consistency with the STLC definitions in
11---     future chapters, it would be better and simpler to
12---     represent numbers by a simple nat, rather than as
13---     strings of `succ` applied to `0` (which also introduces
14---     subtleties that are really not the main point here). But
15---     the present formulation is not a big problem either.
16---
17---     LATER: Harper's lecture from the Milner symposium would
18---     make a good support for this lecture.
19---

21---     offerings of CIS500 that might be wonderful additions to
22---     the TERSE notes.

25-
26--- New topic: *type systems*
27-
28--- - This chapter: a toy type system for a toy language
29-
30---   - typing relation
31---   - *progress* and *preservation* theorems
32-
33--- - Next chapter: *simply typed lambda-calculus*
34-
35--- ## Typed Arithmetic Expressions
36-
37--- - A simple toy language where expressions may fail with
38---   dynamic type errors
39-
40---   - numbers (and arithmetic)
41---   - booleans (and conditionals)
42-
43--- - This means we can write *stuck* terms like `5 + true` and
44---   `if 42 then 0 else 1`.
45-
46--- ### Syntax
47-
48--- Here is the syntax of program terms, informally:
49-
50--- t ::= true
51---     | false
52---     | if t then t else t
53---     | 0
54---     | succ t
55---     | pred t
56---     | iszero t
57-
58--- And here it is formally:
59-
60-namespace TM
61-
62-inductive Tm where
63-  | tru
64-  | fls
65-  | ite (c t e : Tm)
66-  | zero
67-  | succ (t : Tm)
68-  | pred (t : Tm)
69-  | isZero (t : Tm)
70-
71--- #### Notation
72-
73-declare_syntax_cat tm
74--- The keyword atoms (`true`/`false`/`succ`/`pred`/`iszero`) are parsed as bare
75--- identifiers and dispatched in the macro below, rather than declared as
76--- reserved symbols.  Reserving them would break ordinary Lean uses of
77--- `true`/`false` and clash with the constructor/case names `succ`, `pred`.
78-syntax:max num : tm
79-syntax:max ident : tm
80-syntax:75 ident ppHardSpace tm:76 : tm
81-syntax:max "(" tm ")" : tm
82-syntax:max "~" term:max : tm
83-syntax:50 "if " tm:51 " then " tm:51 " else " tm:51 : tm
84-syntax:max "<{ " tm " }>" : term
85-
86-open Lean in
87-macro_rules
88-  | `(<{ $n:num }>) =>
89-      if n.getNat == 0 then `(Tm.zero)
90-      else Macro.throwErrorAt n "the only numeric literal in this language is 0"
91-  | `(<{ $x:ident }>) =>
92-      match x.getId.toString with
93-      | "true"  => `(Tm.tru)
94-      | "false" => `(Tm.fls)
95-      | _ => `($x)   -- a bare identifier is a spliced Lean term (usually a variable)
96-  | `(<{ $f:ident $e:tm }>) =>
97-      match f.getId.toString with
98-      | "succ"   => `(Tm.succ <{ $e }>)
99-      | "pred"   => `(Tm.pred <{ $e }>)
100-      | "iszero" => `(Tm.isZero <{ $e }>)
101-      | _ => Macro.throwErrorAt f s!"unknown operator `{f.getId}`"
102-  | `(<{ ($e) }>) => `(<{ $e }>)
103-  | `(<{ ~$e }>)  => pure e
104-  | `(<{ if $c then $t else $e }>) => `(Tm.ite <{ $c }> <{ $t }> <{ $e }>)
105-
106--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: printing terms back
107-
108-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Parenthesizer in
109-/-- Re-inserts parentheses in `tm` output according to the grammar's precedences. -/
110-@[category_parenthesizer tm]
111-def tm.parenthesizer : CategoryParenthesizer | prec => do
112-  maybeParenthesize `tm true wrapParens prec <|
113-    parenthesizeCategoryCore `tm prec
114-where
115-  wrapParens (stx : Syntax) : Syntax := Unhygienic.run do
116-    let pstx ← `(tm| ($(⟨stx⟩)))
117-    return pstx.raw.setInfo (SourceInfo.fromRef stx)
118-
119-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
120-/-- Rebuild `tm` concrete syntax from a `Tm` term. -/
121-partial def delabTmInner : DelabM (TSyntax `tm) := do
122-  let stx ←
123-    match_expr ← getExpr with
124-    | Tm.tru => `(tm| $(mkIdent `true):ident)
125-    | Tm.fls => `(tm| $(mkIdent `false):ident)
126-    | Tm.zero => `(tm| 0)
127-    | Tm.succ _ => do `(tm| $(mkIdent `succ):ident $(← withAppArg delabTmInner))
128-    | Tm.pred _ => do `(tm| $(mkIdent `pred):ident $(← withAppArg delabTmInner))
129-    | Tm.isZero _ => do `(tm| $(mkIdent `iszero):ident $(← withAppArg delabTmInner))
130-    | Tm.ite _ _ _ => do
131-        let c ← withAppFn <| withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
132-        let t ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
133-        let e ← withAppArg delabTmInner
134-        `(tm| if $c then $t else $e)
135-    | _ => do
136-        -- A bare variable prints without the `~` escape; anything else keeps it.
137-        match ← delab with
138-        | `($i:ident) => `(tm| $i:ident)
139-        | e => `(tm| ~$e)
140-  (⟨·⟩) <$> annotateTermInfo ⟨stx.raw⟩
141-
142-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
143--- The keys are the constants' full names: `Tm` lives in namespace `TM`, and the
144--- `delab` attribute does not resolve its argument against the current namespace.
145-@[delab app.TM.Tm.tru, delab app.TM.Tm.fls, delab app.TM.Tm.zero, delab app.TM.Tm.succ,
146-  delab app.TM.Tm.pred, delab app.TM.Tm.isZero, delab app.TM.Tm.ite]
147-partial def delabTm : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
148-  guard <| match_expr ← getExpr with
149-    | Tm.tru => true | Tm.fls => true | Tm.zero => true
150-    | Tm.succ _ => true | Tm.pred _ => true | Tm.isZero _ => true
151-    | Tm.ite _ _ _ => true | _ => false
152-  match ← delabTmInner with
153-  | `(tm| ~$e) => pure e
154-  | e => `(<{ $e }>)
155-
156--- END DETAILS
157-
158--- #### Values
159-
160--- *Values* are `true`, `false`, and numeric values (`0`, and
161--- `succ` of a numeric value).
162-
163-inductive Tm.IsBValue : Tm → Prop where
164-  | tru : Tm.IsBValue <{ true }>
165-  | fls : Tm.IsBValue <{ false }>
166-
167-inductive Tm.IsNValue : Tm → Prop where
168-  | zero : Tm.IsNValue <{ 0 }>
169-  | succ (t : Tm) (h : Tm.IsNValue t) : Tm.IsNValue <{ succ t }>
170-
171-def Tm.IsValue (t : Tm) : Prop := Tm.IsBValue t ∨ Tm.IsNValue t
172-
173--- ### Operational Semantics
174-
175--- -----------------------------                 (ifTrue)
176---                    if true then t1 else t2 ⟶ t1
177-
178---                    ------------------------------                (ifFalse)
179---                    if false then t1 else t2 ⟶ t2
180-
181---                               t1 ⟶ t1'
182---             -----------------------------------------------      (ifStep)
183---             if t1 then t2 else t3 ⟶ if t1' then t2 else t3
184-
185---                               t1 ⟶ t1'
186---                          -------------------                     (succStep)
187---                          succ t1 ⟶ succ t1'
188-
189---                            -----------                           (predZero)
190---                            pred 0 ⟶ 0
191-
192---                             IsNValue v
193---                         ------------------                       (predSucc)
194---                         pred (succ v) ⟶ v
195-
196---                               t1 ⟶ t1'
197---                          -------------------                     (predStep)
198---                          pred t1 ⟶ pred t1'
199-
200---                           ----------------                       (isZeroZero)
201---                           iszero 0 ⟶ true
202-
203---                              IsNValue v
204---                       ------------------------                   (isZeroSucc)
205---                       iszero (succ v) ⟶ false
206-
207---                               t1 ⟶ t1'
208---                        -----------------------                   (isZeroStep)
209---                        iszero t1 ⟶ iszero t1'
210-
211-section
212-set_option hygiene false in
213-local notation:40 t:41 " ⟶ " t':41 => Tm.Step t t'
214-inductive Tm.Step : Tm → Tm → Prop where
215-  | ifTrue (t1 t2 : Tm) : <{ if true then t1 else t2 }> ⟶ t1
216-  | ifFalse (t1 t2 : Tm) : <{ if false then t1 else t2 }> ⟶ t2
217-  | ifStep (c c' t2 t3 : Tm) (h : c ⟶ c') :
218-      <{ if c then t2 else t3 }> ⟶ <{ if c' then t2 else t3 }>
219-  | succStep (t1 t1' : Tm) (h : t1 ⟶ t1') : <{ succ t1 }> ⟶ <{ succ t1' }>
220-  | predZero : <{ pred 0 }> ⟶ <{ 0 }>
221-  | predSucc (v : Tm) (hv : Tm.IsNValue v) : <{ pred (succ v) }> ⟶ v
222-  | predStep (t1 t1' : Tm) (h : t1 ⟶ t1') : <{ pred t1 }> ⟶ <{ pred t1' }>
223-  | isZeroZero : <{ iszero 0 }> ⟶ <{ true }>
224-  | isZeroSucc (v : Tm) (hv : Tm.IsNValue v) : <{ iszero (succ v) }> ⟶ <{ false }>
225-  | isZeroStep (t1 t1' : Tm) (h : t1 ⟶ t1') : <{ iszero t1 }> ⟶ <{ iszero t1' }>
226-end
227-
228-scoped notation:40 t:41 " ⟶ " t':41 => Tm.Step t t'
229-
230--- ### Normal Forms and Values
231-
232--- The first interesting thing to notice about this `Tm.Step`
233--- relation is that the strong progress theorem from the
234--- Smallstep chapter fails here. That is, there are terms that
235--- are normal forms (they can't take a step) but not values
236--- (they are not included in our definition of possible
237--- "results of reduction").
238-
239--- Such terms are *stuck*.
240-
241-def Tm.IsNormalForm (t : Tm) : Prop := _root_.IsNormalForm Tm.Step t
242-
243-def Tm.IsStuck (t : Tm) : Prop := Tm.IsNormalForm t ∧ ¬ Tm.IsValue t
244-
245--- ### Exercise (2 stars): some_term_is_stuck ⭐⭐
246-
247-theorem some_term_is_stuck : ∃ t, Tm.IsStuck t := by
248-  sorry
249-
250--- However, although values and normal forms are *not* the same
251--- in this language, the set of values is a subset of the set
252--- of normal forms.
253-
254--- This is important because it shows we did not accidentally
255--- define things so that some value could still take a step.
256-
257-theorem nvalue_is_nf (t : Tm) (h : Tm.IsNValue t) : Tm.IsNormalForm t := by
258-  induction h with
259-  | zero => intro hc; obtain ⟨t', hstp⟩ := hc; cases hstp
260-  | succ t0 hn0 ih =>
261-      intro hc; obtain ⟨t', hstp⟩ := hc
262-      cases hstp with
263-      | succStep _ t1' h => exact ih ⟨t1', h⟩
264-
265--- ### Exercise (3 stars): value_is_nf ⭐⭐⭐
266-
267--- (Hint: You will reach a point in this proof where you need
268--- to use an induction to reason about a term that is known to
269--- be a numeric value. This induction can be performed either
270--- over the term itself or over the evidence that it is a
271--- numeric value. The proof goes through in either case, but
272--- you will find that one way is quite a bit shorter than the
273--- other. For the sake of the exercise, try to complete the
274--- proof both ways.)
275-
276-theorem value_is_nf (t : Tm) (h : Tm.IsValue t) : Tm.IsNormalForm t := by
277-  sorry
278-
279--- The "other way" mentioned in the hint proves the same fact
280--- by induction on the term itself rather than on the evidence
281--- that it is a numeric value. It goes through, but is a bit
282--- longer than the `nvalue_is_nf` route above.
283-
284-theorem value_is_nf' : ∀ t, Tm.IsValue t → Tm.IsNormalForm t := by
285-  sorry
286-
287--- ### Exercise (3 stars): step_deterministic ⭐⭐⭐
288-
289--- Use `value_is_nf` (here, `nvalue_is_nf`) to show that the
290--- `Tm.Step` relation is also deterministic.
291-
292-theorem step_deterministic : Deterministic Tm.Step := by
293-  sorry

301--- (A) Yes (B) No

326-
327--- (Hint: Notice that the `Tm.Step` relation doesn't care about
328--- whether the expression being stepped makes global sense — it
329--- just checks that the operation in the *next* reduction step
330--- is being applied to the right kinds of operands.)
331-
332--- Note to developers (mwhicks1):
333---     `In the Rocq source these were a hidden, never-uncommented draft
334---     (with `eval` still to be renamed to `step`).  Here they are activated as
335---     live Lean. Not sure if we want to keep this.`
336-
337--- Suppose we define an alternate single-step relation, written
338--- `t ⇢ t'`, that *drops* the `Tm.IsNValue` premise from the
339--- `predSucc` and `isZeroSucc` rules — so `pred (succ t)` and
340--- `iszero (succ t)` may step even when `t` is not a numeric
341--- value. (It is built with exactly the same notation setup as
342--- `Tm.Step`; note `predSucc`/`isZeroSucc` no longer take a
343--- premise.)
344-
345-section
346-set_option hygiene false in
347-local notation:40 t:41 " ⇢ " t':41 => Tm.AltStep t t'
348-inductive Tm.AltStep : Tm → Tm → Prop where
349-  | ifTrue (t1 t2 : Tm) : <{ if true then t1 else t2 }> ⇢ t1
350-  | ifFalse (t1 t2 : Tm) : <{ if false then t1 else t2 }> ⇢ t2
351-  | ifStep (t1 t1' t2 t3 : Tm) : t1 ⇢ t1' →
352-      <{ if t1 then t2 else t3 }> ⇢ <{ if t1' then t2 else t3 }>
353-  | succStep (t1 t1' : Tm) : t1 ⇢ t1' → <{ succ t1 }> ⇢ <{ succ t1' }>
354-  | predZero : <{ pred 0 }> ⇢ <{ 0 }>
355-  | predSucc (t1 : Tm) : <{ pred (succ t1) }> ⇢ t1
356-  | predStep (t1 t1' : Tm) : t1 ⇢ t1' → <{ pred t1 }> ⇢ <{ pred t1' }>
357-  | isZeroZero : <{ iszero 0 }> ⇢ <{ true }>
358-  | isZeroSucc (t1 : Tm) : <{ iszero (succ t1) }> ⇢ <{ false }>
359-  | isZeroStep (t1 t1' : Tm) : t1 ⇢ t1' → <{ iszero t1 }> ⇢ <{ iszero t1' }>
360-end
361-
362-scoped notation:40 t:41 " ⇢ " t':41 => Tm.AltStep t t'
363-
364--- Some questions about this relation (answers inline):
365-
366--- - Is `⇢` deterministic
367---   (`∀ t t' t'', t ⇢ t' → t ⇢ t'' → t' = t''`)? No:
368---   `pred (succ (pred 0))` steps to both `pred 0` (by
369---   `predSucc`) and `pred (succ 0)` (by `predStep`, since
370---   `pred 0 ⇢ 0`).
371-
372--- - Is every `Tm.Step` normal form also a `⇢` normal form? No:
373---   `pred (succ true)` is stuck for `Tm.Step` but steps under
374---   `⇢` (to `true`, by `predSucc`, now that the `Tm.IsNValue`
375---   premise is gone).
376-
377--- - Is every `⇢` normal form also a `Tm.Step` normal form? Yes —
378---   `Tm.Step` is a subrelation of `⇢`, so anything stuck for `⇢`
379---   is stuck for `Tm.Step`.
380-
381--- - Is every value reachable by `Tm.Step` (in many steps) also
382---   reachable by `⇢` (in many steps)? Yes, for the same
383---   subrelation reason.
384-
385--- - Conversely? No: `iszero (succ true)` reaches the value
386---   `false` under `⇢` but is stuck under `Tm.Step`.
387-
388--- A *functional* version computes a single `⇢` step of a term,
389--- returning `none` when the term is a `⇢` normal form. This is
390--- a nice chance to see a step *function*, which the chapter
391--- otherwise gives only as a relation:
392-
393-def alt_simplify_step (t : Tm) : Option Tm :=
394-  match t with
395-  | <{ if t1 then t2 else t3 }> =>
396-      match alt_simplify_step t1 with
397-      | some t1' => some <{ if t1' then t2 else t3 }>
398-      | none =>
399-        match t1 with
400-        | <{ true }>  => some t2
401-        | <{ false }> => some t3
402-        | _           => none
403-  | <{ succ t1 }> =>
404-      match alt_simplify_step t1 with
405-      | some t1' => some <{ succ t1' }>
406-      | none     => none
407-  | <{ pred t1 }> =>
408-      match alt_simplify_step t1 with
409-      | some t1' => some <{ pred t1' }>
410-      | none =>
411-        match t1 with
412-        | <{ 0 }>       => some <{ 0 }>
413-        | <{ succ t2 }> => some t2
414-        | _             => none
415-  | <{ iszero t1 }> =>
416-      match alt_simplify_step t1 with
417-      | some t1' => some <{ iszero t1' }>
418-      | none =>
419-        match t1 with
420-        | <{ 0 }>       => some <{ true }>
421-        | <{ succ t2 }> => some <{ false }>
422-        | _             => none
423-  | _ => none
424-
425--- `pred (succ true)` steps under `⇢` (the dropped `IsNValue` premise) even
426--- though it is stuck under `Tm.Step`:
427-example : alt_simplify_step <{ pred (succ true) }> = some <{ true }> := rfl
428-example : alt_simplify_step <{ if true then 0 else succ 0 }> = some <{ 0 }> := rfl
429-example : alt_simplify_step <{ 0 }> = none := rfl
430-
431--- ### Typing
432-
433--- *Types* describe the possible shapes of values.
434-
435--- Here are the formal rules.
436-
437-inductive Ty where
438-  | bool
439-  | nat
440-
441-syntax:max "<{ " "⊢ " tm " ⦂ " ident " }>" : term
442-syntax:max "<{ " "⊢ " tm " ⦂ " "~" term:max " }>" : term
443-
444-section
445-set_option hygiene false in
446-local macro_rules
447-  | `(<{ ⊢ $t ⦂ $T:ident }>) =>
448-      match T.getId.toString with
449-      | "Bool" => `(Tm.HasType <{ $t }> Ty.bool)
450-      | "Nat"  => `(Tm.HasType <{ $t }> Ty.nat)
451-      | _      => `(Tm.HasType <{ $t }> $T)
452-  | `(<{ ⊢ $t ⦂ ~$T }>) => `(Tm.HasType <{ $t }> $T)
453-
454--- The actual definition, written in the notation above.
455-inductive Tm.HasType : Tm → Ty → Prop where
456-  | tru : <{ ⊢ true ⦂ Bool }>
457-  | fls : <{ ⊢ false ⦂ Bool }>
458-  | ite (t1 t2 t3 : Tm) (T : Ty)
459-      (h1 : <{ ⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool }>) (h2 : <{ ⊢ t2 ⦂ T }>) (h3 : <{ ⊢ t3 ⦂ T }>) :
460-      <{ ⊢ if t1 then t2 else t3 ⦂ T }>
461-  | zero : <{ ⊢ 0 ⦂ Nat }>
462-  | succ (t1 : Tm) (h : <{ ⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat }>) : <{ ⊢ succ t1 ⦂ Nat }>
463-  | pred (t1 : Tm) (h : <{ ⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat }>) : <{ ⊢ pred t1 ⦂ Nat }>
464-  | isZero (t1 : Tm) (h : <{ ⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat }>) : <{ ⊢ iszero t1 ⦂ Bool }>
465-end
466-
467--- The same rules repeated with hygiene enabled, for use after the section.
468-macro_rules
469-  | `(<{ ⊢ $t ⦂ $T:ident }>) =>
470-      match T.getId.toString with
471-      | "Bool" => `(Tm.HasType <{ $t }> Ty.bool)
472-      | "Nat"  => `(Tm.HasType <{ $t }> Ty.nat)
473-      | _      => `(Tm.HasType <{ $t }> $T)
474-  | `(<{ ⊢ $t ⦂ ~$T }>) => `(Tm.HasType <{ $t }> $T)
475-
476--- Print `Tm.HasType`/`Ty` values back as `<{ ⊢ … ⦂ … }>` notation: `delabTy`
477-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
478-@[delab app.TM.Ty.bool, delab app.TM.Ty.nat]
479-def delabTy : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
480-  match_expr ← getExpr with
481-  | Ty.bool => `($(mkIdent `Bool):ident)
482-  | Ty.nat  => `($(mkIdent `Nat):ident)
483-  | _ => failure
484-
485-@[app_unexpander Tm.HasType]
486-def Tm.HasType.unexpand : Lean.PrettyPrinter.Unexpander
487-  | `($_ <{ $t }> $T:ident) => `(<{ ⊢ $t ⦂ $T }>)
488-  | `($_ $t:ident $T:ident)  => `(<{ ⊢ $(⟨t.raw⟩) ⦂ $T }>)
489-  | `($_ $t $T)              => `(<{ ⊢ ~$t ⦂ ~$T }>)
490-  | _ => throw ()
491-
492-example : <{ ⊢ if false then 0 else succ 0 ⦂ Nat }> :=
493-  .ite _ _ _ _ .fls .zero (.succ _ .zero)
494-
495--- Typing is a *conservative* (or *static*) approximation to
496--- behavior.
497-
498--- In particular, a term can be ill typed even though it steps
499--- to something well typed.
500-
501-example : ¬ <{ ⊢ if false then 0 else true ⦂ Bool }> := by
502-  intro hc; cases hc with | ite _ _ _ _ h1 h2 h3 => cases h2
503-
504-example :
505-    ¬ <{ ⊢ if iszero (succ 0) then succ false else true ⦂ Bool }> := by

513--- ### Canonical forms
514-
515--- The following two lemmas capture the fundamental fact that
516--- the definitions of boolean and numeric values agree with the
517--- typing relation: a well-typed value of type `Bool` is a
518--- boolean value, and of type `Nat` a numeric value.
519-
520-theorem bool_canonical (t : Tm) (hT : <{ ⊢ t ⦂ Bool }>) (hv : Tm.IsValue t) : Tm.IsBValue t := by
521-  cases hv with
522-  | inl hb => exact hb
523-  | inr hn => cases hn with
524-    | zero => cases hT
525-    | succ t0 h => cases hT
526-
527-theorem nat_canonical (t : Tm) (hT : <{ ⊢ t ⦂ Nat }>) (hv : Tm.IsValue t) : Tm.IsNValue t := by
528-  cases hv with
529-  | inl hb => cases hb <;> cases hT
530-  | inr hn => exact hn

532--- ### Progress
533-
534--- The typing relation enjoys two critical properties.
535-
536--- The first is that well-typed normal forms are not stuck — or
537--- conversely, if a term is well typed, then either it is a
538--- value or it can take at least one step. We call this
539--- *progress*.

567-

570--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
571---     Check the typesetting of this...
572-
573--- *Theorem*: If `⊢ t ⦂ T`, then either `t` is a value or else
574--- `t ⟶ t'` for some `t'`.
575-
576--- *Proof*: By induction on a derivation of `⊢ t ⦂ T`.
577-
578--- - If the last rule in the derivation is `ite`, then
579---   `t = if t1 then t2
580---       else t3`, with `⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool`,
581---   `⊢ t2 ⦂ T` and `⊢ t3 ⦂ T`. By the IH, either `t1` is a value
582---   or else `t1` can step to some `t1'`.
583-
584---   - If `t1` is a value, then by the canonical forms lemmas and
585---     the fact that `⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool` we have that `t1` is a boolean
586---     value (`Tm.IsBValue`) — i.e., it is either `true` or
587---     `false`. If `t1 = true`, then `t` steps to `t2` by `ifTrue`,
588---     while if `t1 = false`, then `t` steps to `t3` by `ifFalse`.
589---     Either way, `t` can step, which is what we wanted to show.
590-
591---   - If `t1` itself can take a step, then, by `ifStep`, so can
592---     `t`.

628--- ### Type Preservation
629-
630--- The second critical property of typing is that, when a
631--- well-typed term takes a step, the result is a well-typed
632--- term (of the same type).

643--- ### Exercise (3 stars): finish_preservation_informal ⭐⭐⭐
644-
645--- Complete the following informal proof.
646-
647--- *Theorem*: If `⊢ t ⦂ T` and `t ⟶ t'`, then `⊢ t' ⦂ T`.
648-
649--- *Proof*: By induction on a derivation of `⊢ t ⦂ T`.
650-
651--- - If the last rule in the derivation is `ite`, then
652---   `t = if t1 then t2
653---       else t3`, with `⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool`,
654---   `⊢ t2 ⦂ T` and `⊢ t3 ⦂ T`.
655-
656---   Inspecting the rules for the small-step reduction relation
657---   and remembering that `t` has the form `if ...`, we see that
658---   the only ones that could have been used to prove `t ⟶ t'`
659---   are `ifTrue`, `ifFalse`, or `ifStep`.
660-
661---   - If the last rule was `ifTrue`, then `t' = t2`. But we know
662---     that `⊢ t2 ⦂ T`, so we are done.
663-
664---   - If the last rule was `ifFalse`, then `t' = t3`. But we know
665---     that `⊢ t3 ⦂ T`, so we are done.
666-
667---   - If the last rule was `ifStep`, then
668---     `t' = if t1' then t2 else t3`, where `t1 ⟶ t1'`. We know
669---     `⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool` so, by the IH, `⊢ t1' ⦂
670---           Bool`. The `ite`
671---     rule then gives us `⊢ if t1' then t2 else t3 ⦂ T`, as
672---     required.
673-

686--- ### Type Soundness
687-
688--- Putting progress and preservation together, we see that a
689--- well-typed term can never reach a stuck state.
690-
691-def Tm.MultiStep (t1 t2 : Tm) : Prop := Multi Tm.Step t1 t2
692-
693-scoped notation:40 t1:41 " ⟶* " t2:41 => Tm.MultiStep t1 t2
694-
695-theorem soundness (t t' : Tm) (T : Ty) (hT : <{ ⊢ t ⦂ T }>) (hm : t ⟶* t') : ¬ Tm.IsStuck t' := by
696-  induction hm generalizing T with
697-  | refl a =>
698-      intro hst; obtain ⟨hnf, hnv⟩ := hst
699-      cases progress a T hT with
700-      | inl hv => exact hnv hv
701-      | inr hs => exact hnf hs
702-  | step a b c h1 h2 ih => exact ih T (preservation a b T hT h1)
